My hon. friend told me a couple of days ago that he would have to obtain supply earlier than usual this year, as there was a strong probability that the Senate would be rising. There have been oppositions sitting in this House, with which my hon. friends across the way are familiar, that have taken an absolutely different stand, apparently under the impression that sharpshooting and sniping and anything of that sort were admissible in the game. We have the idea that our function ought to be to enable the government properly to carry

on, and we know that it is necessary that these bills should 'be passed a little in advance in order that the public service may be continued. I therefore give my full and free consent, so far as I am concerned, to the bill going through on the usual terms. I am agreeing to-day to the payment in advance of one-sixth of the estimates. subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION EOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED

speechtext: The House resumed, from March 13, the adjourned debate on the motion of Hon. T. A. Low (Minister of Trade and Commerce) to ratify and confirm a contract between His Majesty and Sir William Petersen providing for the establishment of a subsidized steamship line on the Atlantic, and government control of certain ocean rates, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Clark (Burrard).

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION EOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of one of the races comprising this great British Empire, may I affirm our kindly feelings and good wishes to all those who are to-day commemorating their patron saint.
Now, Sir, I feel no apology is necessary for participating in the discussion of the subject now before the House. The proposition as placed before us by the government requires our careful consideration. It is one of universal importance because it affects each one of us directly or indirectly. Commerce and transportation are the most important subjects that can be laid before any parliament. Every great nation has achieved greatness through use of ocean routes, and therefore I say I have no apology to offer in discussing a subject of this importance. The report before us suggests a combine among the north Atlantic shipping interests. This is an American word implying a restriction of trade or commerce, a restriction that may extend even to the point of becoming a monopoly. But the report gives us no definite proof that there is any such combine or restriction of competition. If, however, we grant the existence of a combine, we must admit that three great principles lie at the basis of its discussion. The first is, that contracts in restraint of trade- which is rather a local word, implying business between parts of a country or adjoining states-and contracts in restraint of commerce -which is a wider term-are very undesirable. The second principle is, that the economic effects of such a restraint may be either good or evil. The third principle which should be discussed by any such report is, that antitrust legislation very often oversteps its scope and produces harmful effects. These three principles find no part in the report or in the (discussion of the subject so far by members of *the government. Therefore, when the report goes to the committee, we as a House must insist that there shall come back to us some proof that there has been a restraint of trade

Ocean Shipping Rates
or lessened competition; in the second place, a description of the effects, whether good or evil, of such restraint; and third, what will be the ultimate result of the solution proposed by the government.
I come now to the attitude which would be assumed by the man in the street as he discusses with his fellow men the proposal put forward by the government to offset the alleged combine among the north Atlantic shipping interests. The first question he takes up, as far as we have been able to come in touch with him, is the attitude of the agent of the government in the preparation of his report and his solution of the difficulty. Heaven forbid that I should apply to the author of the report the description given by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) -a good mouser This phrase brings before us two characters of the feline family common to any home. One is the family tabby with sleek fur, comfortably ensconced in the living room, decorated with pink and blue ribbons and a favorite with every member of the household and every visitor. This animal is not a mouser-is not expected to be one. She is welcomed to the best couch and is the family pet. The other character is the cat who comes only occasionally, satisfies his intestinal craving for the good things of life, then hears the call and jumps out into the backyard. He is the disturber of the backyard peace, his screams annoy the sleeping world, and his portion is a mixture of bricks, bottles, boots and bones, and as he flies from yard to yard he makes trouble not only for himself but all his race. He does not set out to find any particular trouble, 'but he creates it wherever he goes. Finally he comes 'back home, tired and disreputable, scolded by all the family except the old grandma sitting in the comer; she takes him up, defends him for all his bad actions and says, " He is a good mouser." And now this member of the feline family comes home again: he has moused in Japan, he has moused in China, he has moused in Korea, he has moused in England, he has moused in northern Europe; but at last he is back home once more, battered and tom, and the old grandmother again takes him upon her lap and she says, " Well, this is our family cat; we have raised him, we are responsible for all his wilful ways, and we must keep him, for he is a good mouser."
I could leave the subject there, because we are not concerned with the past, or anything else, of the agent in this matter; but we must look at his present conduct. And the man in the street, when he reads his morning's paper, finds that this agent of the government, just 78

after reaching home, gives an interview. This is the character of the interview as set forth in the Ottawa papers:	Speaking of his work
and his visit overseas, he says:
I see that Sir George MacLaren Brown, the Canadian Pacific Railway's steamship representative in London, is criticizing me for not having called upon him while I was there. Why should I be bothered with a mere subordinate when the head offices of the company are right here in Canada?
And he goes on:
I want to laugh when I read the suggestion that the facts should have been referred to Sir Norman Mackinder, chairman of the North Atlantic Shipping conference. They might just as well be referred to a certain well-known newspaper, which is simply a mouthpiece of the corporations. If the government were so foolish as to place the issue in his hands, I would be amazed. In any case, why should we do so? It's none of their business.
Then he goes on:
There is one important thing I notice to-day in the cable news. It intimates that Petersen will not get the £600,000 subsidy which he was entitled to simply because he proposes to enter into competition with the combine. If that's the case, it's the first body blow to Imperial preference, and I am right ready to join with those who will end the farce of this so-called preference for good and all time.
Now, that is hardly the attitude that should be taken by a representative of the Dominion government who goes abroad to discuss a matter of such vital importance. The men mentioned in his report are strong men, they have done good work, and there should be no attempt to initiate a warfare between this country and these interests. We need one another; they need us and we need them in this great work, if there is to be development in this country in the matter of commerce and transportation.
In the second place, the man in the street questions this report as 'likely to defeat the object which the government has in mind. If the government's attitude is to prevent the lessening of competition, they have taken a rather doubtful method of accomplishing that. Through all ages the factor that has always prevented a monopoly of ocean routes has been the tramp steamer, and instead of encouraging the tramp steamer this proposal is likely to have the opposite effect, is likely to take away business that the tramp steamer would otherwise get. The tramp steamer has always had an important place in the development of commerce. If you take the figures as given lately you will find that visitations of tramp steamers have been very frequent and have been increasing so far as the ports of this country are concerned. In Montreal in 1921 there were 301 tramps; in 1922, 409; in 1923, 246; and last year 447. In further evidence as to the importance of
Ocean Shipping Rates

the tramp you will find these words in volume I, The Merchant Navy, by Hurd:
The importance of the tramp owner in the shipping economy of the Empire cannot be too much emphasized. "Not only was he responsible for the larger part of our steam tonnage, but we were dependent on him for the import and export especially of what may be termed the rougher class of bulk cargoes, which are not as a rule suitable for liner business. It would be impossible for a country like the United Kingdom, with its enormous flow of trade, to depend wholly on regular lines with scheduled sailings."
I think I voice the opinion of the man in the street when I say that the government's proposal will not assist in the development of the tramp business. In further evidence that the tramp business plays an important part in British trade I would like to refer to figures given in 1914 with respect to steamships engaged in overseas trade. There were 1,200 regular liners at the beginning of the war, in 1914, having an average tonnage of over 5,000, and there were at the same time 2,400 tramps having an average tonnage of
4,000.	It would seem to me as if the encouragement of the tramp, looking at the matter from the Dominion as well as the imperial standpoint, would be the better solution of the problem of lessened competition or restraint in commerce, if there is such.
The third point that the man in the street would take up is the fact that this solution offered by the government barely gives us a service. If you will turn to pages 12 and 15 of the fifth annual report of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine you will find that of our sixty ships twelve were engaged in sailings between Canada and Europe. These twelve ships were able to provide only a fortnightly sailings to Bristol and fortnightly sailings to London and Antwerp. If twelve ships can give only a fortnightly service it is hardly to be expected that the service will be very much increased by ten ships. In connection with the services given by these twelve ships the question arises, what about our attitude toward the Canadian Government Merchant Marine? Will the merchant marine be simply set aside? And, in the second place, what will 'be the attitude of the larger interests which we would antagonize by this proposal? It is a serious question for us to consider, and the committee should be able to give us the attitude of the government along these lines.
The fourth point that the man in the street takes up in regard to this proposal is the question, who is to get the benefit of it? If it is a matter of control of ocean rates, then any advantage in that direction would assuredly affect the Old Country, whatever

indirect benefit we would get therefrom, and the taxpayer of Canada would have to pay. We do not see that the Old Country is at present burning with an enthusiastic desire to get at the solution of this question or to assist in connection with the measure that the government now proposes.
I understand the hon. member to refer to the possibility of the British consumer benefiting by this subsidy. Would he make that a little clearer for us?

My point is this:
the man in the street, looking at this proposal, says: Here we are paying over a million dollars a year for ten years, for whose benefit? To control ocean rates, if possible to reduce them, largely for the consumer in the Old Country. True, we will get indirect benefit from it by increased commerce. But to the man in the street it looks as though we were paying for cheaper rates for the consumer in the Old Country. Why the Old Country may not become as enthusiastic as we expect in this matter I shall endeavour to point out a little later. Just now I am endeavouring to show how these proposals appear to the ordinary Canadian citizen, the man in the street, and these questions must be answered later on when this matter comes back to us.
The man in the street is also struck by this fact in regard to this proposal. From one end of this country to the other cries are going up to-day not only to this government but to every government in the Dominion of Canada for retrenchment and economy; and how are we answering those cries? We are answering them by the proposed building of a road to Hudson bay, by a road through the Peace river country, by two roads into the Rouyn country, where perhaps one would do. We see no effort, not even an attempt at economy. On the other hand, this government is met from day to day with cries as to the condition of the workingmen of this country. The condition is brought home to the government, that no matter who is to blame, whether it is the men on strike or the interests who are culpable, a large section of this country is to-day in want. It may be said that that is a provincial matter, but I would like to point out this: The health of the people of any part of this country is not a provincial matter; it is a national matter, and if there are conditions in this country Where women are suffering,^ where children are cold and 'hungry, then it is a matter that will sooner or later affect us as a country. Children without proper food and

Ocean Shipping Rates
nourishment must suffer from the effects of malnutrition, rickets, and the onset of tuberculosis. Women worried about the condition of their family must sooner or later develop neurotic and neurasthenic conditions which will affect the women of this country as a whole. This government, instead of paying heed to the cries of economy and retrenchment, are building hotels in Paris, and sending out $3,000,000 of our money for that purpose; they are buying a club in London, and sending out $2,000,000 more for that; they are building up the ship yards of another country to the extent of $13,000,000 of our Canadian money, when the work could very wdll be done at home. The question of economy and retrenchment must come before the man in the street when he is considering the entrance of the government into a proposition involving an expenditure of $13,000,000.
The other night the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) in discussing this subject brought forward the argument that the Old Land had refused to consider this proposition or enter info a conference on the matter. I would like to-day for a short time to take up with this House the position that Great Britain occupied during those years 1909 and 1910 and down to 1914. I want to give reasons why in my opinion Great Britain could not enter into a conference or consider the matter at that time. And I would like to say that these are my own opinions; they may be wrong, but at the same time I look upon this matter as an Imperial problem.
The first objection that Great Britain would have against going into a fight on this matter would be that for ages she herself had granted just such monopolies to different parts of the empire. These monopolies were for very special state reasons. There was the East India Company, for instance; the West India Company, the Hudson Bay Company, and so on. She could not very well criticize interests for doing what she as a state had been doing. Her further reasons for non-interference would take us into a discussion of the position of the British mercantile marine and its importance as a factor in the development of Great Britain's commerce. Great Britain's existence has always been bound up in her merchant marine. For her own defence this merchant marine, we might say, started with special privileges she had given to, what were known as the Cinque ports, and to the merchants of those ports.
It is interesting to note three or four events which show how dependent Great Britain has 78i
been upon the development of her merchant marine. There was first, in the Norman days, the battle of Sandwich in which the fleet consisting only of British seamen on British merchantmen defeated a French armada from Calais which was about to make a descent on England under Eustace the Monk. In 1217, there was the battle of Sluys in which, near Bruges, the British fleet, made up altogether of merchantmen from all parts, destroyed a French and Genoese fleet about to make a second descent upon Britain. In 1415 the first fleet raised by the Henrys was raised altogether from vessels around the ports of Great Britain. The fourth event was the aggregation of vessels which composed the English fleet which defeated the great Armada. Throughout the middle ages, you find the merchant marine not only maintaining but even extending the trade of the empire, and, as well, providing all the means for defence and security of the country. That brings us down to the Napoleonic period, which ended in 1815, and it is important to note the part that was played in that great conflict by the British mercantile fleet. In the Napoleonic wars these merchants of Great Britain lost some eleven thousand vessels by capture, and yet in spite of that at the end of 1815 they had 24,860 vessels upon the ocean. In 1874 they had 36,900, and of these 24,828 belonged to the United Kingdom. These figures indicate the persistence of the merchant people of Great Britain in the face of great losses, and also the assistance they gave in carrying their country through great crises. They indicate the part that was taken by the merchants and by the merchant marine of Great Britain in the affairs of state, and in the development of commerce and in the defence and security of the empire. Following 1815, there came a period of re-organization, with practically no assistance from the state. Its inspiration was due to farsighted and resourceful business men in the great British seaports. In spite of war, in spite of enemies and the interference of press gangs, the merchant marine continued to grow. This covers a hundred years of development, from 1815 to 1913 in which one of the chief items of importance in regard to the development of our merchant marine was the enactment of "navigation laws" which embodied a principle of absolute protection. These laws confined the import trade to British ships or ships of the producing country, restricted the carriage and transportation to the colonies, and reserved the whole of the coasting trade to British vessels navigated by British masters and with crews seventy-five per cent British subjects. In 1823 these laws were repealed.
Ocean Shipping Rates

The year 1850 was a very marked year in the development of our merchant marine. In that year the Marine department of the Board of Trade was formed. This department concerned itself with the question of security at sea, and with the proper type of sailors and seamasters. This century witnessed the transformation from sailing to steam vessels which at first retarded the development of the merchant marine, 'but later the occurrence of the American Civil war removed competitors from the trade and it was found that British tonnage, from 1850 to 1874, had increased from 65 to 68 per cent, while the United States tonnage in foreign trade had fallen from 60 per cent to 38 per cent. But this is the point I am coming to. The Prussian tonnage only varied from 49 to 46 per cent becoming a very important factor in competition with our British mercantile marine.
The 'duty of the Marine department of the British Board of Trade was clearly defined and restricted; it was concerned mainly in providing for the security of life and property at sea. It had no share directly in the upbuilding of the mercantile marine; in fact state interference-I should like the House to note this, because this is the important point -state interference With trade either by land or by sea was regarded with suspicion and distrust: The strength of the merchant marine has always depended, in the main, upon the enterprise and business ability of the shipowning community in meeting the nation's needs without state subventions or state encouragement. The relations between the government and the mercantile marine have also *been very close, so that in August, 1914, the Admiralty controlled a naval reserve of upwards of 18,000 trained officers and men of the mercantile marine and fishing industry, in addition to a total of 170,000 men of the marine of British birth and 100,000 British fishermen. During the sixty years preceding the outbreak of the war the Board of Trade, Lloyd's Register and ship owners shaped the valuable economic and warlike weapon which proved an essential element to victory when at last the great war opened.
In 1890 the United Kingdom had 3,000,000 tons of sailing vessels. In 1900 this had declined to 2,000,000 tons, and in 1913 it had dropped to 850,000 tons but between 1885 and 1913 there was built up some 25,000,000 tons of steam shipping. Two-thirdS of this was constructed in the United Kingdom and over one-half for the British flag. At the same time shipping had increased during this period-1894 to 1913-from 700,000 tons to
2,000,000 tons. Great as this growth was in

British tonnage-and in the attempt to meet the increased shipping Britain had nearly doubled her tonnage between 1903 to 1913; in the same period the increase in Germany was four fold. It was a fortunate occurrence that Great Britain possessed half the merchant shipping of the world at the beginning of the war, otherwise the Motherland would have been seriously hampered in its prosecution of it and the ultimate result .might have been different. At this date-the opening of the war-the British merchant marine was the largest, most modern, and most efficient of all the merchant navies of the world. Its quantity was divided as follows: In the United Kingdom 11,538,000 tons, and in the colonies and dominions 902,000 tons, making a total of 12,440,000 tons, whereas the world's total was only 26,000,000 tons. The nearest competitor at that time was Germany with
3,096,000	tons.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these facts show the *critical periods in the history of the British Empire, largely the history of our mercantile marine. It was just at these criti-4 p.m. cal years-between 1890 and 1913 

that Britain was asked to take part in a conference which would affect her standing in relation to this great shipping which had 'been built up largely by the sacrifices, by the persistence, and by the tenacity of the merchants of her ports and the seamen on her shores. If we had a "mouser" of some importance, some one with some knowledge of the history of British shipping and of the relation between Great Britain and her mercantile fleet, one who could go into these questions seriously and bring to this House the report as to whether we can now or at any time in the future take any action which will interfere with the relationship which has always existed' between the merchant navy and the state, we should be in a better position to consider what steps we should take. This relation to which I have referred is a serious question and requires a great deal of consideration by this or any other government. The period of crisis when Great Britain was asked to take part in this' conference is past. To-day there is a spirit of co-operation abroad, there is a spirit of Imperial development moving; and what was refused then might well be considered at this present time, and I have no doubt will be considered.
Now, I come to two practical suggestions in dealing with this subject. The government has expressed the opinion that no suggestions have been offered by hon. gentlemen on this side. Well, I am going to offer one now. We can take no steps, with safety and security to

Ocean Shipping Rates
this country, that will interfere with the great work that Great Britain has carried out in the last hundred years. If we want to take part in the development of a marine that will go on in the future I suggest, 'as some other members of this House have suggested, that our attitude should be a most friendly one towards the Canadian Pacific mercantile marine. That marine has no intention of acting in any way that will prejudice Canada's prosperity. Their interests are bound up completely in Canada; their whole development, their future, will depend upon the future of Canada; and we could very well consider the building up by the Canadian Pacific of a .marine that would be a credit to us in the future. Second, there is the support that we could get from our Canadian Government Merchant Marine. I am not one who will discredit the merchant marine; I believe that with good management a service could be obtained from it. There are no' reasons why boats cannot be properly fitted out, and, I would like to bring to the attention of the government a case in 1899 and 1900 when the government of Canada made use of boats such as existed then to carry troops, cavalry and artillery to South Africa. We went out on one of the Elder-Dempster line, hastily brought into the port of Halifax and prepared in such a way that she carried some 600 horses to South Africa. That voyage lasted about twenty-six days, and no doubt these horses suffered somewhat on the voyage. But on a voyage to the Old Country of twelve days or two weeks, no such injury could be effected to animals, 'cattle or horses. There is no use in saying that our merchant marine could not be used. These Elder-Dempster boats of which I have spoken were only ordinary merchant marine boats, not nearly as good as the boats we have now, and they were fitted up at that time for the purpose of transport to South Africa.
I should like to conclude my remarks by a summary of my position in regard to this matter:
1. The attempt of a state to break a conference of commercial interests engaged in shipping is a most difficult one.
'2. The attempt of a state such as Canada, deeply in debt, which attempt is complicated already by a heavy burden of transportation now on our shoulders, seems almost futile.
3.	The Petersen contract is a reversion to the old monopolies of the middle ages when the state granted trading privileges to certain of its citizens as a monopoly, which monopoly is now given by way of cash bonuses.
4.	Canada's future will be best served by co-operation with her own interests and the use of her own merchant marine rather than by going out of our borders to build up a marine service which will not be ours.
5.	Canada's future will also be well served by a development of a connection which will serve to defend as well as to extend our commerce.
There is no future for Canada in the proposed contract with the government. At the end of ten years, which is a long period in the life of an individual, but a very short period in the life of a nation, we shall have developed a unit which is not our own, upon which we shall have spent some thirteen million dollars odd, and in doing this, we shall not have developed work in our own country where there is a great need of such work.
In the amendment there is the possibility, or the appearance, of imperial action, of imperial co-operation, and it is at least worthy of our best consideration.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Kingston (Mr. Ross) will, perhaps, excuse me if I do not attempt to follow him in detail in the remarks which he has just made. He has summarized his views in a few concluding statements, and to these I shall make a brief reply. My hon. friend feels that this attempt is one which," under the circumstances, is likely to be difficult, and therefore, I gather from his remarks, should not be proceeded with. That is a counsel of despair. To meet a situation, that is, we admit, very difficult and complicated, it offers nothing, whereas the very fact that the task is difficult and complicated, makes it, we feel, a task that should not be left untouched, but one for the government of this country to undertake. My hon. friend says that he fears the attempt which we are making will be futile. I am amazed that, speaking, as so many from my hon. friend's side have spoken, in support of the shipping interests, they should feel the great concern they do about this attempt, if it is to turn out as futile as my hon. friend claims. As a matter of fact, if proof were needed that it is necessary to make such an attempt as the government is making at the present time to meet a grave situation, it will be found in the extensive propaganda which has been spread from one end of this land to the other, through the press of the country by the shipping interests. What astonishes one at the moment is their finding such great need-as shown by the efforts they are making -to oppose the so called Preston report. If
Ocean Shipping Rates

this plan that the government proposes is to be futile and of no avail, what are these powerful interests so much concerned about? There come to one's mind the saying: "The lady doth protest too much, methinks." In this instance, the shipping interests are helping to direct attention to the necessity and vastness of the situation with which the government is attempting to cope.
My hon. friend made a somewhat quaint comment to the effect that he regarded the government's action as a reversion to some mediaeval form of bestowing a monopoly. When one has listened, as we have been forced to listen for some days past to remarks of hon. gentlemen opposite, to the effect that this is a sort of popgun scheme, as I think one hon. member expressed it, a hay-rake attempt, as some other hon. members expressed it, one cannot but marvel at the "mediaeval" monopoly that is being given to this Petersen fleet of ships in face of the great monopoly with which it purports to contend. My hon. friend says that he thinks the country would be better served by developing the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. If that is the case, why, when his leader was in office and that particular overture was made to him by members of his own administration and his high commissioner in London,-why did not he attempt to put the merchant marine in action and have it serve the useful purpose which his worthy followers now says he thinks it might be capable of serving? A little later on I shall have something to say about the merchant marine and its effectiveness in this regard. My hon. friend thinks the time would be better spent in developing a connection that would defend as well as extend our commerce. I hope that before I conclude my remarks, I shall show my hon. friend that that double aim will be achieved by the method which the government is adopting. Finally, he remarked that in the amendment there was a possibility, and then he very wisely modified the word and said, the appearance, at least, of imperial concern, or interest, or control, in the course which had been suggested by the amendment. My hon. friend showed his usual caution when he used the word "appearance," because that is, I think, the extent of the control the amendment promises.
I come now more directly to the resolution which is before the House and the amendment which has been moved with respect thereto. The resolution is the first necessary step to be taken by the government preliminary to the introduction of a bill to give the
TMr. Mackenzie King.]
government control of ocean rates. The resolution relates to the control of ocean rates; that is the principle underlying it, and hon. members in voting upon the resolution are passing on the important question whether or not in their opinion the government should undertake to control ocean rates. Whether the method which the government is taking to control ocean rates may be effective or not is a subject which, I think, admits of debate and which should be discussed fully and carefully. But I would point out in that connection that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low), when he moved the resolution, took care to intimate to the House that the agreement which the government has made with Sir William Petersen with respect _ to placing on the Atlantic the ten ships mentioned, will be sent to a special committee of this House, together with the bill in which it is included, for full consideration, and that hon. members will have the opportunity afforded by such a select committee to weigh carefully all sides of that agreement, and to pass upon it, only after they have thoroughly considered it.
May I point out that it would not have been possible for the government to bring this important question to the attention of the House and refer it to a committee in any effective way other than the way that has been adopted, namely, by preparing an agreement.
Do I understand the Prime Minister to say that he proposes that a bill shall be brought in and referred to the committee? Is that bill to be based on this resolution?

For fifteen or twenty years there has been a suggestion that something should be attempted in the way of a joint control of ocean shipping on the part of the different empire units, but as I say nothing has been done. I might say immediately that over and over again the Associated Chambers of Commerce of Great Britain have suggested this very thing. If they, with all the power they represent, have been unable to get the Imperial Shipping Board to take action of the constructive kind which has been suggested, does my hon. friend, or do any other hon. members, think that action is going to be taken by that board at the request of this chamber? I do not think my hon. friend from Burrard (Mr. Clark), although he presented the amendment, ever drafted it. We are all familiar with the drafting of my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) opposite, and I will pay him the compliment of saying that it was he who drafted the amendment in the language in which it now appears.

and I am going to use plain, bald Anglo-Saxon-is that it is untrue, and I ask hon. members to vote against it for that reason. It says:
-and the contract made -by the government with Sir William Petersen, based on the report of W. T. R. Preston, is ill-advised, costly and futile, and unworthy of the serious consideration of this House.
Let me say to the House, the contract was not based on the report of Mr. Preston. This statement in the amendment is therefore wholly incorrect and is absolutely untrue. One does not need to go further than to look at the dates of the two documents and see that. Take the contract itself. If hon. members will look at that document they will find that it is dated December 11, 1924; if they will look at the Preston report they will find that it is dated December 31, 1924, several days-weeks in fact-after the contract itself had been signed. There is the first evidence that the statement is not true. But take Mr. 
Preston's own statement that appears on pages 11 and 12 thereof. There is a communication, called "frank statement Canadian case" presented in the form of a memorandum to the shipping interests of Great Britain. This statement is dated London, April, 1924. Let me read the statement to the House:
The Canadian government has decided to take action in order that Canadian interests shall not be so seriously affected as heretofore by the operations of the North Atlantic steamship combine.
Of two phases of the situation, the government has taken particular notice:
(1)	The occasional discrimination in freight rates against Canadian ports and in favour of United States ports.
(2)	Freight rates which are believed to be excessive in connection with the carrying of natural tproducts and manufactured articles to overseas markets.
One of the reasons alleged for the discrimination against Canadian .ports is that the insurance rates are higher in the St. Lawrence river than to or from American ports. The government has this question under serious consideration and is hopeful of permanently establishing a parity of insurance rates on the St. Lawrence with those to and from American ports. So that phase of the question need not be commented upon. There are two solutions of the disadvantages under which the ocean transportation of Canadian products labours:
(1)	By an arrangement with an independent steamship company with government assistance, and government control over freight rates.
(2)	The establishment of a government service between British and Canadian ports with modern vessels.
The former is regarded as the more desirable, if satisfactory arrangements can be effected.
One or other of these alternative solutions is regarded by many interests in Canada as. inevitable.
During the session of parliament, 1923, a committee of the House of Commons heard evidence on the question of the North Atlantic steamship combine, and in reporting to the House of Commons, recommended the government to take action with a view of overcoming the disadvantages connected with the transportation of Canadian products overseas.
This recommendation moved by Mr. A. R. Mc-Master, chairman of the committee, was unanimously approved by the House of Commons in the session of 1923.
In accordance with the instructions of parliament, the government has been making inquiry into the various phases of the question.
There is a statement made by Mr. Preston to the effect that as a result of the resolution of the House of Commons, based upon the report of a select committee of the House, the government had decided to take action, and that that action would be taken in one or other of two forms. The first is discounted at the outset, namely, the undertaking of a government-owned merchant marine. The other is that the government would be prepared to make a contract with a company that was ready to give to the government in return control over ocean rates on its lines. There in Mr. Preston's own report is the announcement that the government had decided upon the course which it was about to take before Sir William Petersen had even been heard of.

Ocean Shipping Rates
Sir William Petersen was given the contract because he was one of several persons approached who was prepared to enter into a contract' with the government giving them control over ocean rates on his ships.
And may I say here, Mr. Speaker, that the government has made it known from the outset that it was prepared to make a similar contract with any shipping company in this country that was prepared to give it like terms. The government to-day is prepared to give the Canadian Pacific Steamship Company and other steamship companies doing business out of Canadian ports, the opportunity of entering into a contract along identical lines with the Petersen contract, if they are prepared to do the same as Sir William Petersen is prepared to do, namely, give this government control over the rates on the commodities which they take overseas.
May I ask the right hon. gentleman a question? Was such an offer extended to the Canadian Pacific Company prior to the Petersen contract being drawn up?

If they do not come along and accept our offer, what is the obvious explanation? The one explanation is that these lines to-day find it more profitable to operate the way they are operating

I do not say whether they are operating within a combine or not-otherwise they would be willing to give the government of this country control of ocean rates under conditions similar to those of this contract. rates on its service. The two things are very different.

Will the right hon. gentleman allow me a question? Is he prepared to say that he will do the same with any other company? In other words, will he give a subsidy of 816,000 odd per voyage to boats of this size?

I have made that very clear. I have limited my remarks to Canadian companies, but I have said that for the present any Canadian company that will give a similar service and similar rights to the government will be given similar treatment. Can I make it any clearer than that? More than that, it would not be fair to ask. This discussion about subsidies, as generally understood, is all beside the mark when one understands the significance of the contract that the government has entered into. A little later I will make a reference to some of the present subsidies being paid in this country-subsidies to steamships performing regular services and exacting the rates which the combine permits them to exact. That is not what we are doing under the contract with Sir William Petersen. Sir William Petersen has offered to put certain ships on the Atlantic, but not with money paid by the taxpayers of this country, as hon. gentlemen opposite are so fond of saying. So sure is he of the ability to make returns- knowing as he does the exactions of this ocean combine-that he says: "I am prepared to put on the Atlantic ten steamers of the most up to date type and to give the government of Canada the right to fix the rates at any figure they like, in consideration of a certain guarantee that they give me at the start,"-which guarantee has been mentioned. Now, I ask hon. members to think that matter over. You cannot get something for nothing; you have got to pay in one way or another for whatever you want. Is it not worth while paying something to discover whether or not these allegations about the operations of an ocean combine are true? We will soon discover that once this contract goes into force; we will soon discover whether or not Sir William Petersen is able to carry his agreement out. If he is able to carry it out; if he is able to save the producers of this country millions of dollars for the consideration he has received, having regard to the rates at which he is prepared to have commodities carried, and can still make a profit, it null not be long before the people of this country, the people of the Old Country, the people of Australia, South Africa and New

Until some government is strong enough and fearless enough to launch such a project and to demonstrate to all parts of the empire the actual conditions in respect of this combine-or conference, whatever it may be called-on the Atlantic whereby rates are controlled,-until that step is taken you will never get the different parts of the empire to work in concert in 'an effort to control rates. May I now, Mr. Speaker, answer the question: Why has the government taken the course it has?-What has been the genesis of the contract that the government has entered into? First of all I would point out that this subject has been one of the most important subjects before this country not during the last two or three years only but during the last ten or fifteen years, at least. The matter of high ocean rates has been the subject of investigation by royal commissions in this country and in the Old Country, by special commissions and special committees. I shall not go over their findings in detail, but I will refer hon. members to the following important documents which will show whether or not there is reason for believing that a combine does exist on the Atlantic for the purpose of controlling rates and' keeping them at an unduly high figure. There was a royal commission on Shipping Rings appointed by the British government in 1906, which made its report in 1909. There was the Dominions

Ocean Shipping Rates
Royal Commission appointed pursuant to a resolution proposed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier at the Imperial conference in 1911 and unanimously adopted. That commission was appointed on April 15, 1912, and reported finally on February 21, 1917. In 1913 the hon. member for West Yorkj (Sir 'Henry Dr-ayton), at that time chairman of the railway commission, was appointed by Sir Robert Borden's government to investigate ocean freight rates, and he made a report on October 18, 1913. If there was nothing to investigate, why did Sir Robert Borden appoint my hon. friend, choosing him because as chairman of the railway commission he had special knowledge of the conditions affecting transportation? In June, 1920, an Imperial Shipping committee was appointed by the British government by virtue of a resolution of the Imperial War conference of 1918. This committee is still in existence and has made reports on various phases of shipping within the empire. During the last year it held sittings in this country through the medium of a subsidiary committee. Then there was the special committee of this House of Commons to inquire into agricultural conditions, appointed on February 28, 1923. This committee submitted seven reports to the House, those concerned with ocean freight rates being the fourth report, submitted on April 23, 1923, and the fifth report, submitted on June 18, 1923.
I have in my hand the report prepared by my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton). That report was made as far back as 1913, and I find in it this statement:
The Canadian exporter, by reason of the fact that, speaking in a general sense, nearly all the country's exports have a low value in proportion to the space occupied, and a comparatively low value in relation to the cost of transportation, is peculiarly affected by any increases in the cost of transportation, so that it becomes a matter of prime importance to keep such costs to a reasonable rate.
Then at page 8 I find this:
I have no doubt, however, that on articles sold on the Canadian market by the British exporter in close competition with exporters in other countries, the increases in rates of recent years has a detrimental and injurious effect on the traffic, and may account in part for the falling ratio of British exports.
So, away back in 1913 my hon. friend from West York opposite reported to the government of that day an increase of rates on the Atlantic ocean which he believed was having an "injurious effect" upon exports. I will show that the view which my hon. friend then took is the view which has been consistently taken by all who have made careful inquiry from that day down to the present time. The only difference is that hon. gentlemen opposite
have done nothing, whereas this government has attempted to grapple with the problem.
May I make this reference to Mr. Preston's report? When my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) received a communication from Sir George Perley, High Commissioner for Canada in London, in January, 1921, drawing his attention to Sir Robert Borden's efforts to have ocean rates investigated, and telling my right hon. friend that he thought the matter should be investigated, there was in connection with that letter an intimation that if any success were to attend the investigation it was desirable to have someone prepare the Canadian case with a view to assisting in its presentation, in association with Sir George Perley, before the Imperial Shipping committee. What did my right hon. friend do? He appointed someone. He appointed Professor Magi'll, just exactly as we appointed Mr. Preston, to gather information in regard to Canada's case. But here is the difference. My right hon. friend said to me the other day that that report of Mr. Magill must be in the department.
No, I did not.

situation. The 'difference between his administration and ours is that there he left the matter, he did not pursue it a step further, for reasons best known to himself; but this government took care to bring into the House of Commons, apart altogether from Mr. Preston's report, a concrete proposal, and we intend to see that both are submitted to the special committee which will be appointed to look into this matter.

The demand for investigation made by the Canadian government and acceded to as above noted by the Imperial authorities, is therefore justified by the exigencies of the traffic moving in either direction.
And he concludes:
This affirmation-
He is referring here to something that was stated earlier:
This affirmation by a member of the Conference of a condition under which the business of any given importer could, at any time, perhaps by the carrier's whim, Jack of information, or desire for an excessive return, be at least temporarily extinguished, would appear of itself to call for the fullest investigation.
In other words, the hon. member for West York found in 1913 a condition whereby producers and other exporters in this country might have their business extinguished at the whim or caprice of the organization controlling affairs on the Atlantic at that time, and he said very properly that such a condition demanded investigation. Is not that in itself sufficient ground for a step such as the government has taken at this time.

Conditions committee in its report suggest that further work along this line should be undertaken by Mr. Preston?

Your committee are of the opinion that upon the regular steamship lines trading from Canadian ports the price of transportation service is determined neither by the law of supply and demand, nor on the basis of cost plus a reasonable profit, but that a combine exists among the various shipping companies, which combine is known as the North Atlantic and United Kingdom Conference Eastward-bound.
Now, that is not Mr. Preston; that is a committee of this House composed of hon. members of this House who held an inquiry under oath and who found that a combine existed. It was on the strength of that report that the government proceeded; and it is by virtue of that report, amongst other documents to which I shall refer later that the government has taken the action which it has seen fit to take in this matter. The report goes on to show how this Liner committee operates. Perhaps I had better read the paragraph:
The general rates were set at the North Atlantic and United Kingdom Conference in New York:
At this point, Mr. Speaker, may I stop to say just a word. My hon. friends opposite when it comes to labour problems, are very strong in urging that these international unions which have their headquarters in the United States should not be permitted to operate in Canada. Over and over again they have made the statement that it was an outrageous thing that Canadian labour should be associated in any way with American labour and that we should be subject to the dictation of American

unions in connection with our industrial affairs. Well, here in regard to the whole shipping business of this country entering into competition with the United States a select committee of this House has found that the rates are fixed in New York.

Is not the most central
point the natural place for a committee controlling the shipping operating in all parts of the Atlantic?

speechtext: My hon. friend has admitted the whole case. He says there is a committee operating over the whole of the Atlantic and that New York is the natural place for it to meet.
