My hon. friend (Mr. Bristol) -who knows pretty intimately, I think he will admit, the workings of the steamship companies, has told the House that there is a conference that operates on the Atlantic, and it is a world-wide conference.
Is it not a natural place for it to be? Would you have it in Montreal?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, all I am anxious to point out to the House is that we have been contending, and hon. gentlemen opposite have been disputing our contention, that there is a conference that controls ocean rates-that the whole of the cattle and other trade from this country is subject to the action of that conference-and it is in order to take away from that world-wide combine with headquarters at New York the determining of the rates that shall be paid for ocean transport that we propose to take a step which will at least ensure that so far as that part of the trade between this country and the Old Country is concerned it shall be subject not to the control of New York but to the control of the government of Canada. There is the whole purpose of the government's proposal. The alternative is perfectly plain. After what my hon. friend has just said, no hon. member of this House can plead any ignorance whatever of the situation. It has been admitted here this afternoon that there is a world-wide conference controlling rates on the ocean, and that those rates are controlled from the city of New York. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bristol) has admitted that Canada is subject to rates fixed in New York in that way. Now, the House can rest content with that state of affairs, or it can seek to have the control of ocean rates vested in the government of Canada so that in regard to the export trade of this country the determination of rates- whether it refers to matters great or matters small-shall not be left to the United States but shall be left to the representatives of the
Canadian people themselves or persons authorized by them to act in their name.

Is it the right hon. gentleman's idea that the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, who are members of this conference are American bodies? In view of the fact that the government merchant marine has been a member of the conference right up to the present time why have you not obtained a report from its management during the last three or four years so that you might see what kind of a robber that marine has been, that is if you say the members of the conference are robbers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think that my hon. friend's latest remark in any way affects the force of the statements I have made.
You are forced to trust to the use of our own merchant marine.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will touch upon the merchant marine a little later. In reference to this point all I want to make clear now-so that hon. members will appreciate the fact as they consider the wisdom of the step the government has taken-is that a committee of this House has 5 p.m. already found and reported to the House the facts. It has arrived at the following finding, and I am quoting from the report of the special committee itself:
The general rates were set at the North Atlantic and United Kingdom Conference in New York, but for the purpose of united action in regard to these and other -matters, a weekly meeting was held, at which representatives of all the steamship lines attended. At this meeting, rates were agreed upon, and no member of the line had the right to depart from the rates so established without conferring with and warning its competitors of his intention so to do. An earnestly worded expostulation would be directed by one member to another if this line of conduct was not followed.
This state of affairs brought about the following extraordinary result. The government of the United States forced the shipping board of that country which manages the United States govemmentally-owned steamers, to make a very low rate for the transportation of Sour to Europe-a rate stated by the shipping companies to be below a commercial rate.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This rate applied only to flour ground in the United States. To meet this rate, the North Atlantic Conference lines established, at a given moment, a rate of fifteen cents per hundred pounds on flour ground in the United States, while they -maintained a rate of nineteen cents per one hundred pounds on Canadian flour-a very substantial differential against our Canadian millers.
Ocean Shipping Rates

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Why does my hon. friend not now say hear, hear?
The United States government forced their own boats to give this special rate to United States shippers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
To this agreement as a member of the North Atlantic Conference, the Canadian Merchant Marine was a party.
Now what is the statement made there? That the United States government itself found it necessary to take action against this combine in regard to its own vessels, and the action which was taken affected the price of flour so far as the United States shipper was concerned. What affect did it have so far as Canada is concerned? It left Canadian millers at a disadvantage in regard to shipments to the Old Country. How great that disadvantage was I shall have occasion to show before proceeding very much farther. Take a further statement:
Evidence was produced showing that since the commencement of the war, ocean rates on cattle had increased by 300 per cent, while the price of beef in the British market had only increased 66 per cent during the same period.
Is that not a fact of which this House should take cognizance?
Is that out of the committee's report?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is part
of the report of the committee of which my right hon. friend, along with other members of this House approved.
Now there was a fifth report, and it is on these reports that the government's action has been based^not on any report by Mr. Preston, but on reports made by a select committee of this House. On Monday June 18, 1923. the select committee appointed to inquire into agricultural conditions presented their fifth report. Here is the first paragraph of it:
The special committee appointed to inquire into agricultural conditions beg leave to present the following as their fifth report:
Ocean freight rates
In their fourth interim report, your committee dealt with the question of ocean freight rates, the control of the rates charged by liners trading out of eastern Canadian ports by the North Atlantic and U.K. Conference, eastward bound, and the operations of the Canadian liner committee, sometimes called the weekly liner committee.
In view of the paramount importance of this subject and of statements made in the press and elsewhere concerning the findings of your committee, we feel that the matter merits further attention.
This is the paragraph that follows:
That the transportation business, as far as concerns ocean liners is very largely in the hands of rings or

conferences is a matter which admits of no possible successful contradiction.
There is the finding of this special committee that made a further investigation into the question of high ocean rates, and it states in language as emphatic as it is possible to put into a report that the transportation business as far as the ocean liners are concerned centres very largely in the hands of rings or conferences. That is a matter which admits of no possible successful contradiction. I might read other parts of the report but it would only be in corroboration of the quotations which I have just given.

Will the Prime
Minister read the recommendations contained in the seventh and final report of the committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Well, my hon. friend-

The report which
the Prime Minister is quoting, to my knowledge, was never submitted to the committee at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.friend may read anything he wishes to the House, but he will perhaps permit me to conclude what I was reading. On page 17 of the report there are quotations from the report of the inquiry of the Dominions Royal Commission which, of course, took place many years ago. These statements all1 go to substantiate the fact that the condition with respect to the control of ocean rates by these shipping rings found here to-day is a condition which existed many years ago. Then the report says:
In spite of the lengthy investigations held into this subject-
And this is interesting in connection with the matter now before the House; this is at page 19,-
-no definite government action either on the part of the British authorities or on the part of the Canadian authorities has yet been taken.
A suggestion is made-I think it is a very wise one and this might be as appropriate a time as any to point it out-in connection with the amendment that has been moved that this control should be by all parts of the empire working together, that if a control of' all these ocean rings is to be completely effective, something even larger than the bringing together of the different parts of the British Empire is necessary. As a matter of fact, it- will take something in the nature of international control, joint action on the part of all countries in the world interested in shipping, to effect complete control. That day may be far distant; but if

Ocean Shipping Rates
there is to be effective control, that will probably be the only means whereby it will be ultimately attained. Mr. Lubin, President of the Agricultural Institute at Rome, I think, made the suggestion in connection with the grain and cattle trade, that there should be some method of effecting international control. I venture to suggest that this is a subject which the League of Nations might well take up, and see if it is not possible, through the instrumentality of the League to bring together the different countries of the world in an effort to effect some kind of international control of ocean rates. But these are things that will take many years to accomplish. In the meantime, one step that will help to bring the matter prominently to the fore, as it is being brought prominently to the fore in the world to-day as a result of the action which this government is taking, is to proceed in a concrete manner with some step which will demonstrate whether the allegations that have been made with respect to high ocean rates are or are not correct.
Then the committee found as follows:
Your committee, in view of the foregoing and of the evidence adduced before them and referred to in a previous interim report, are of the opinion that action is desirable to control shipping rings or conferences.
That is precisely what the government is now attempting. It is attempting to carry out the finding of a committee of this House to the effect that action is necessary to control these ocean rates. The step which this government is now taking in this connection is not the first one. The government has grappled with this problem from the start, and it has attempted different means of bringing about the control which the committee placed upon it as an obligation to be met. One of the steps of which no mention thus far has been made was a step taken by my hon. colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low), who himself went to Montreal, asked the shipping companies to meet him there, and asked these shipping companies if they would not co-operate with the government of Canada in an effort to bring down ocean rates with respect to shipments of cattle to the Old Country, that being one of the foremost of the commodities of our country for which since the removal of the embargo we had a new and important market. He asked if they would not cooperate with the government in seeking to gain for the fanning community of this country the market which properly belongs to Canada in Great Britain. But my hon. friend got little in the way of encouragement from the shipping companies. I have in my hand,
from amongst the papers that have been laid on the table of the House, copies of letters which passed between the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the shipping companies with respect to the interviews which he had at that time. This was in March, 1924. Let me read this letter:
White Star Dominion Line
Office of the Manager,
Montreal, February 21, 1924. The Honourable Mr. T. A. Low,
Minister of Trade and Commerce,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:
Referring to your conversation with the writer in regard to the ocean freight rate on cattle and the desire of your department to assist the farmers.
The question was fully discussed yesterday afternoon at a meeting of all the Canadian lines who operate vessels built to carry cattle; but the unanimous decision (was that with the present rate the cattle business is not sufficiently remunerative to attract additional tonnage, and any reduction would mean increased losses and curtailment of sailings.
The last paragraph reads:
We are most anxious to do everything possible to assist the cattle trade in Canada, and consider that the government would be well advised to encourage farmers to raise cattle more extensively; but we very much regret that we cannot see our way to make any further reduction in the ocean rate, which in 1921 was $45, and is now $20 per head.
Your3 very truly,
P. A. Curry,
Manager.
They did not state that at one time the rate was $7 per head. But the Minister of Trade and! Commerce did not let matters drop there. On February 29, 1924, he sent the following communication to Mr. Curry: Dear Mr. Curry :
I acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 21st instant and regret that you have not been able to see your way clear to meet the government in this matter which we had under discussion during my recent trip to Montreal.
I am anxious to have another meeting with you and other prominent shippers before we decide on any other line of action from the government point of view.
I want hon. members to see the significance of that statement. The Minister of Trade and Commerce proceeded on two occasions to Montreal to discuss with the shipping companies some means of getting better rates across the ocean for Canadian cattle into the British market, believing that the Canadian cattle industry is one of the most important of the industries in Canada and one which this government had a special reason for seeking to develop, in view of the fact, that we, at least, were successful in having the embargo against Canadian cattle removed. My hon. friend went on these two occasions, but on neither of them was he able to get any successful accom-
Ocean Shipping Rates

modation on the part of the shipping interests. Mr. Low said:
I am anxious to have another meeting with you and other prominent shippers before we decide on any other line of action from the government point of view. I would be glad to go to Montreal but as this is a very busy time for us with the session on, I would like to know if you could possibly come to Ottawa to see me some day next week. I would be very glad if you would advise me of the same and also whether some of the other shippers could join you. We are anxious to have another discussion of the situation before deciding on our definite line of action.
Yours very truly,
Thos. A. Low.
The correspondence goes on to indicate that Mr. Curry said he thought it would be well to have a representative, to quote his words, "from every Canadian line interested in the cattle movement," meet with Mr. Low. Mr. Low approved that and intimated that he thought, seeing they were all coming together, it would be better for him to go to Montreal and meet- them there. He went to Montreal, and I have a letter here dated March 15 from Mr. Curry to Mr. Low which reads:
I have to thank you for your letter of the 12th instant, and greatly appreciate your offer to come to Montreal to meet the representatives of the cattle lines, and we will be very pleased to see you at any time on Wednesday, March 19, that is convenient to you.
The following gentlemen will probably attend the meeting: Mr. W. A. Coates, The Robt. Reford Co., Ltd. (Cunard-Donaldson Lines), Mr. J. W. Nicoll, Furness, Withy & Co., Ltd. Mr. J. P. Doherty, Canadian Government Merchant Marine. Mr. P. A. Curry, White Star-Dominion Line. . . .
I	am told that Mr. Gear also attended this meeting.
This was a year ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, March of last year. It was because the government found it impossible to get the co-operation of our own Canadian Ship owners in its effort to reduce rates on the Atlantic for cattle, that we took the further step we have taken of seeing if we cou'ld not find some company elsewhere that would foe prepared to cooperate to that end. We were ready to do for these other companies what we are now proposing to do for the Petersen Company, but these gentlemen were unwilling to meet us in that connection.
Will the Prime Minister say that a similar offer was made to them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot say
offhand at the moment what particular offer was made, but I know the minister went prepared to make a very generous offer. He could inform the Housefoetter than I could as

to the nature of it. But the reply that was received gave us reason to believe that the shipping interests were not prepared to consider any offer.
The Prime Minister referred to the Preston report. I hope I do not offend him in referring to it. The suggestion was to pay a share of the cost of the shipments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the
nature of the offer made to the shipping interests was that the government would be prepared to consider a certain payment, in the way of consideration to the companies, if they would fix a price of which the government would approve. If they did that consideration was to be given. And that is the nature of the arrangement we have made with the Petersen company.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon. We have agreed with the Petersen Company that if they will carry cattle, let us say, at a rate which we shall fix they will get the subsidy, and if they do not they shall not receive it. Let the House understand the proposition. What this government has offered to the Petersen Company, and what under this contract the company have agreed to accept, is that the Canadian government shall fix a rate at which cattle are to be carried from all parts of Canada to Great Britain. The company agree to carry cattle, we shall say, at a rate this government will establish.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Did someone
say no?
Yes; I say no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Will the hon.
gentleman give us his reason.

The contract does not
oblige the Petersen Company to carry.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not know what my hon. friend can be talking about; the whole business depends upon the carrying. Sir William Petersen does not get a five cent piece unless he carries.

The contract does not
say so. If the Prime Minister will read it he will find, I submit, that the contract gives Sir William Petersen the control of ocean rates. If I cannot prove that I am willing to accept whatever the right hon. gentleman says.

Ocean Shipping Rates

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend is driven to that point to attack the contract he has got to the last resort.
In the last resort, I say, Sir William Petersen controls the rates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Let me in the name of the government definitely state the position. I desire to make it perfectly clear so that there oan be no misunderstanding. If th' contract does not mean that the government of Canada shall fix the rates, then the government of Canada will have nothing to do with it. My hon. friend's interruption is all beside the mark. What the government purposes to do, once the ships are built, is to tell Sir William Petersen the rate at which he is expected to carry cattle from Canadian ports to the ports of Great Britain. If he carries at that rate he will be paid to the extent provided for in the agreement; but if he does not perform that service he will not be entitled to a five cent piece nor will he get so much as a five cent piece. Gan anything be plainer than that?

But the agreement does
not say so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If it will help my hon. friend at all for me to say so, I may tell him that it does not matter one whit whether the agreement as drafted does or does not say so; what does matter is that the position of the government is precisely as I have stated it and will be so shown before the committee, otherwise to give it effect, the agreement will have to be amended. But I contend that ,the agreement does provide what I have said; that is the purpose of the contract. Let me read paragraph (d!) of section 1:
That the control and regulation of the rates to be charged by the contractor shall rest with the government of Canada and that the government shall fix such transportation rates on all commodities from time to time.
Where does Sir William Petersen get the control of the rates there?

Will not the Petersen
Company be expected to pay a satisfactory dividend on its invested capital? If so, would that factor have a tendency to interfere with the effective control as indicated in the contract?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is absolutely beside the mark. So far as this government is concerned, we do not care whether the Petersen Company pays a dividend or not; what we are concerned about is to see that the company shall carry out its 79
contract. The agreement is that, for the consideration we are to give Sir William Petersen, he is prepared to let us fix the rate at which commodities are to be carried. Let me point out that this contract has been drawn up by as able a counsel as can be found in the Dominion of Canada; I think that Mr. Lafleur's name commands a position in the legal profession in this country second to none.
Was he acting for Canada or for Petersen?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He was acting for the Dominion of Canada. He was retained by the government and instructed to prepare a contract which should place no liability on the government of this country, in the event of the service which it calls for not being adequately performed.

Was he told to relieve Sir
William Petersen too of liability?	*

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think that the government would have suggested such a thing to him? Would the hon. gentleman himself have made such a suggestion?

I cannot gather from the right hon. gentleman's remarks what he has in mind; but I say most emphatically, and I am satisfied that he will agree with me, that Sir William Petersen will not remain responsible under this contract. And the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) did say, in reply to a question I put to him, that he considered that feature vital. I venture to say that no one who has any knowledge of law, or who appreciates the effect of clause 1, will say that Sir William Petersen will remain responsible under any covenant he gives in the first instance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is my hon. friend's view, but he will find that he is mistaken.

I would ask another question. Do I understand the right hon. gentleman to say that he contends otherwise? To make it plain, does he contend that, under clause 1, when the proposed company is formed Sir William Petersen may not be relieved of his covenant, or of all covenants, for that matter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend will have a chance to examine Sir William Petersen when he is before the committee.
But I-

Order.

Ocean Shipping Rates

Let us be reasonable. The Prime Minister and other hon. gentlemen have suggested that this is one of the most important matters that this parliament has dealt with. Surely, then, it is reasonable that a member of this House should ask the leader of the government whether or not he does contend that Sir William Petersen will be responsible under the contract. Does the Prime Minister say that when the company is formed and Sir William Petersen's contract is superseded by one with a new concern, Sir William Petersen will not be totally relieved of every covenant in the agreement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My understanding is that he will be responsible.
And Mr. Lafleur so advised.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes; Mr. Lafleur so advised. But apart from that altogether, let us assume that what my hon. friend says is correct. If Sir William Petersen were to get out of the contract and some other company should take it over, not a single dollar of the money of the Canadian people will go to anyone until the service is performed in accordance with the contract. That is the vital point. If Sir William Petersen makes an arrangement with some company to take over the contract, as I presume he may do, if he is a wise man, seeing that he may not live out the period of ten years, the fact remains that the contract calls for a certain class of ships and for a regular service to be rendered from Canadian ports, continuous and at certain rates to be fixed by the government. No payment will therefore be made until that service is performed. What difference does it make whether some other company takes over the contract or whether Sir William Petersen personally carries it out?
Mr. BOYS. Does the Prime Minister want an answer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend has not spoken yet and he will get his opportunity.
If the right hon. gentleman-
Order.
If the Prime Minister says that he does not want to be asked questions I certainly will not ask him any.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am glad to have questions asked.
That is all I am doing.
Don't make speeches.

I simply want to know whether the government places any reliance on the financial standing of Sir William Petersen. If it does, surely in the event of his being relieved of the contract it would be a matter of consequence whether the succeeding company were financially sound or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
So far as the
government is concerned, may I say that in this whole matter we have taken into consideration the circumstance that not a dollar of public money will be paid out of the treasury until service is performed in accordance with the terms of the contract which has been entered into with Sir William Petersen. The question whether Sir William himself or some company that may take over this contract from him will perform its terms is a secondary matter altogether. What I think this House and the Canadian public is interested in knowing is whether there will be liability so far as the government of Canada is concerned where the service has not been performed. Now, I wish to state emphatically in the name of the government that if this contract means in any particular that payments are to be made other than as service is performed, the government will not entertain the contract for an hour. The obligation is clear, it is there in black and white: What we are paying for is the right to control rates. Let us get down to a concrete case. We started, as I have been intimating, dealing with tile question of rates on cattle. One of the last letters sent to Mr. Low, Minister of Trade and Commerce, was from Montreal on May 9, 1924. It says:
Dear Mr. Low,-Referring to our conversation in this office on Wednesday last, the question of cattle rates has been given further careful consideration, but I regret to have to advise you that none of the lines owning vessels which carry cattle are prepared to make any reduction in the present ocean rate which, as you are aware, is $20 par head.
Yours truly,
P. A. Curry,
Manager,
White Star Dominion Line.
Mr. Low replied on May 13, 1924, as follows:
Dear Mr. Curry : Acknowledging receipt of your letter of May 9, may I say that I greatly regret that your company and others have not been able to see their way clear to co-operate with the government in lowering the carrying rates on cattle.
That was all in May of last year. After that Mr. Low himself went to England and made inquiries to see if he could find a steamship company in the Old Land which was prepared to carry cattle at a lower rate for a consideration. My hon. friends want

Ocean Shipping Rates
to see how this contract was developed. There is the development of it. The government had made up its mind that it would, if possible, effect an arrangement whereby the cattle of this country could be transported to the British market at a lower carrying charge than was exacted by the steamship lines. We sought in every direction, and the outcome of that search-it was difficult-was the offer made by the Petersen company to undertake the work. May I say to hon. members that I discussed with Sir William Petersen very closely how he expected for the consideration which we were paying to be able to make this arrangement go. His reply to me at each stage was, "Mr. King, if I did not know the charges which are being made by this ocean combine at the present time I would hesitate to make an arrangement of the kind; but if you can tell me anything about ocean rates that I don't know, I will be glad to be told." In other words, Sir William Petersen believes that he can demonstrate not only to this country but to Great Britain and the world that he can let this government -I put it concretely-cut rates on cattle from $20 to $15 or even to $10 per head for the consideration that he is getting, and .deliver those cattle in the markets of Great Britain. Now, is it worth while attempting that in the interests of the Canadian people?
What is the position? For thirty years or more our cattle have been shut out of the British market. Away back in the early nineties, through an alleged violation of some cattle diseases act, our cattle were excluded from that market. No one took very seriously the reason alleged viz., that Canadian cattle suffered from pleuro-pneumonia, or whatever the disease was. The measure was looked upon as disguised protection for the cattle interests of the Old Land. Government after government in this country from that date onward sought to have the embargo removed. The late government sought to have it removed. I do not wish to claim particular credit for this government, beyond drawing attention to the fact, that through the activity of Hon. Mr. Larkin, the High Commissioner, I believe more than anyone else, this government was able to bring about a change in the situation, and the British government did do away with the embargo on Canadian cattle. What did we find? Although we had secured the right to ship Canadian cattle to the British market, we found that rates being charged for ocean carriage were such that we did not begin to get the number of cattle across that we had every reason to expect 'would be exported. Having that market at our doors, this govem-79i
ment has felt that it was worth to the cattle raisers of all provinces of this country payment of a very considerable sum to secure the British market for their cattle. In efforts in that direction my hon. friend (Mr. Low) was seeking to make an arrangement with the shipping companies of Montreal by which it would be worth their while to carry cattle at a lower rate. Finding it impossible to make that arrangement, he went to England and while there secured a conference with the Petersen concern and made the proposal which as developed is as now formulated in the contract before parliament for consideration.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that I have at least made clear the genesis of this matter, I hope I have shown the House that the Preston report was in no way the basis of the agreement made with the Petersen line; but was rather the assembling of material intended to be of service when the matter came up for discussion; and that the actual contract itself was based on findings of a committee of this House and on the needs of the situation as they have been pressed on the government from every direction.
May I now say a word about the representations that have been made to this and preceding governments on the question of ocean rates? While I have spoken more particularly of cattle, ocean rates affect the chances of export of every single commodity produced or manufactured in Canada. There is not an interest of any size in this country, I venture to say, whether it foe the cattle raising interest, the grain producing interest, the milling interest, the lumbering interest, the dairying interest, the fruit and vegetable growing interest, the manufacturing interests or producers or consumers generally, importers and exporters of packages and the like, that has not been making protests year after year to the government of Canada about the way in which business has been held up through the high rates charged on the Atlantic. If the House will give me the time, I purpose to put on the records to-night some of these representations, and the point to which I wish t(o direct the attention of the House before I place them on Hansard is that in virtually every one of the communications, language is used to the effect that unless these ocean rates can be reduced our export business is going to be thwarted and the industries themselves strangled as a consequence. My right hon. friend talks about unemployment, about industries closing down, about men walking the streets,-let him read these documents of which the departments are full, and
Ocean Shipping Rates

many of which have been laid on the table, and he will find that interest after interest of the classes I have mentioned have been representing to the government that their whole export business, through the differentials given on the Atlantic is threatened with extinction. In other words, every one of them has made representations to the effect that the rates from New York to British ports are so much lower than those from Canadian , ports, that there is no hope of their being able to export through Canadian ports. They have directed the attention of the preceding government and of the present government over and over again to these excessive rates which are threatening the existence of the country's export business.
I would ask hon. members to look at the correspondence that was tabled the other day between the government of Canada and the British government in regard to the subject of ocean rates, especially in relation to the Imperial Shipping committee-correspondence that was brought down at the request of my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen). The first letter is signed by Sir George H. Perley, who at the time was High Commissioner in London. It reads in part as follows:
London, S.W., 4th January, 1921.
Dear Mr. Meighen,-You will remember that during the past ten years the question of ocean freight rates has been discussed many times, as they often seemed higher than was reasonable, and some of us thought that a way might be found for controlling them by a body similar to our railway commission. I am sure that you have been approached many times on the subject and I had occasion to look into it a good deal when carrying on the Trade and Commerce department in Ottawa in Sir George Foster's absence. Not long after we came into power, while Acting Prime Minister,
I arranged with Sir Henry Drayton to come over here and try and find out the feeling here on the subject. He came back not feeling very hopeful about the possibility of getting anything done in the direction of freight rate control but he will be able to tell you about this himsdlf.
That was not the first trip of the hon. member for West York across to the other side in connection with this matter. He had gone over in 1913 and had tried to effect some measure of control; then apparently he was sent over in 1918, and, as Sir George Perley says, came back not feeling very hopeful.
I think my hon. friend is making a mistake there. I went over only once on that question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I beg my hon. friendfs pardon; I had assumed that Sir George Perley was Acting Prime Minister at the latter period.
I do not know as to that, but I was over only once.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Then I retract what I said in that regard. At any rate, my hon. friend was over in 1913. Then Sir George Perley goes on:
Nothing was done about this question during the war but on April 29th, 1919, I received the following cable from Sir Thomas White who was then Acting Prime Minister:
"Canada much concerned about ocean freight rates- Inquire and cable whether British government would co-operate with Canada in giving effect to report of Koval Commission on Natural Resources, Trade and Legislation of certain portions empire as presented to Imperial parliament in March, 1917-this report finds that it is not desirable that operations of steamship companies carrying passengers and freight between Canada and England should remain longer without government supervision-most important to obtain official position of British authorities respecting matter."
This I at once communicated to the Colonial Secretary here and I spoke to Sir Robert Borden about it when I was in Paris a few days after receiving it. In the reply from the Colonial Office they drew attention to a despatch which had been sent to the Governor General on December 9th, 1918, and which contained suggestions for the constitution of an imperial investigation board for the purpose of reviewing questions relating to maritime transport and to the development of the sea communications of the empire.
Sir Robert Borden had evidently been giving the matter his careful consideration and in May, 1919, he prepared a memorandum "respecting necessary control of ocean freight rates and the disposition of available shipping," of which you will find a copy attached. This memorandum, which suggested in effect that the control of ocean rates and disposition of shipping should be placed in the hands of a commission, composed ot representatives from the various parts of the Empire, was transmitted to Mr. Lloyd George and to the Prime Ministers of the other Dominions.
I need not read the whole of that communication. It is sufficient to say that first of all Sir Robert Borden, as Prime Minister, then Sir George Perley as Acting Prime Minister, then Sir Thomas White as Acting Prime Minister and afterwards the right hon. leader of the opposition, (Mr. Meighen) as Prime Minister-all four of them attempted to deal with this question, believing that the matter of .high ocean rates was all important. The communication of Sir George Perley, concludes:
As such a large amount of tonnage is owned in these islands-
He was writing from London.
-they are perhaps naturally not very anxious about control of freight rates, and therefore, if you decide to bring the question before the committee, I do not think it possible to give too much time or attention to the preparaion of our case.
Yet what is the amendment that is moved by hon. gentlemen opposite? It is to do the very thing that Sir George Perley says he thinks will not meet with much response on the other side. In his communication to my right hon. friend himself Sir George Perley says:
MARCH 17, iSF-C
Ocean Shipping Rates
As such a large amount of tonnage is owned in these islands they are perhaps naturally not very anxious about the control of freight rates.
Yet my hon. friend drafts an amendment suggesting that we should solve this question by referring it to a commission on the other side. If hon. members will look at the memorandum which was drafted by Sir Robert Borden they will find that the first paragraph is as follows:
As transportation between different portions of the British Empire must be carried on almost wholly by means of shipping the control of ocean freight rates and a just disposition of available shipping in the interests of the whole empire are vitally necessary.
These are emphatic words-"control of ocean freight rates . . . vitally necesisary." That is what we believe; that is what we are seeking to bring about, and we are taking what we believe to be the only steps that can be taken to get results. Sir Robert says in paragraph 6:
In its broadest aspects the question thus presented must necessarily demand attentive, and perhaps prolonged, consideration for its permanent solution; but a temporary solution is urgently important, as beyond question the present situation has become critical and if uncontrolled it will probably lead to unfortunate and perhaps disastrous results.
There Sir Robert Borden gives his views to the British government, those views being communicated by Sir George Perley to the right hon. leader of the opposition. Sir Robert states that control is a vital necessity; that it may take a long time to bring about effective control but that some immediate step is necessary, otherwise the results may be disastrous. That is the exact position the government takes in this matter. We do not contemplate that the arrangement we have entered into with Sir William Petersen will effectively control the ocean rates for all time, but we do believe it is a necessary first step to bring about the kind of control which ultimately will be effective. We think it is at least a beginning, and a beginning in the right direction.
I shall not "with respect to these communications take up the time of the House further than to read a letter which my right hon. friend himself wrote to Sir George Perley in acknowledgment of Sir George's communication. This letter is dated at Ottawa, February 16, 1921, and is as follows:
Dear Sir George Perley,-After consideration of your letter of January 4th we have decided that the question of the control of ocean freight rates should be placed before the Imperial Shipping Committee at an ^arJy date. We also agreed with your suggestion that the case from the Canadian view point should be carefully prepared, and Dr. Magill, of the Grain Exchange, Winnipeg, has been asked to undertake the task. A3
soon as his report and recommendations are received they will be considered and transmitted to you for your guidance.
Yours faithfully,
Arthur Meighen.
The Hon Sir George H. Perley,
High Commissioner for Canada,
19 Victoria Street,
London, S.W.l,
England.
Then in writing Dr. Magill the right hon. gentleman says:
You wiill observe that the Canadian government have attached great importance to the desirability of securing, if feasible, some control of ocean freight rates.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
And he asked Dr. Magill to make a report. My right hon. friend says "hear, hear." But what did he do? This letter was written in February, 1921, and month after month went by without any further attention being paid to the matter by my right hon. friend. He did not press Dr. Magill for his report; he never asked for any report. Moreover, my right hon. friend himself went to England that summer; he attended the meeting of the Imperial conference and he was right next door to where the Imperial Shipping committee was sitting. Does my right hon. friend tell this House that he made any effort to carry out what he was there suggesting might be done in the way of keeping down ocean rates? As a matter of fact my right hon. friend knows that after writing the letter to Dr. Magill he never gave the matter another thought; he let the shipping interests have free sway. So far as the needs of the public were concerned, the matter rested at the point indicated by the quotation which I have just read.
Now, may I point out that my right hon. friend received more representations (than those I have mentioned-and I have quoted from his own colleagues, a pretty strong phalanx, if one stops to think of it: Sir Robert Borden, Sir Thomas White, Sir George Perley and Sir Henry Drayton, four of the best known names in our country, each of them Prime Minister or Acting Prime Minister in his day, each urging that some steps be taken to see that, this matter was remedied. Then we have my right hon. friend's own name added to the list, and we find all of them declaring that this question of ocean rates was something that demanded the attention of the government, but all of them leaving the matter at that point. Now they suggest that we should settle this by referring the whole question to some conference that is to be held in Great Britain.
Ocean Shipping Rates

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext:
I am
strongly opposed to the passing of this bill, the objectionable features of which should be apparent to every hon. member. As outlined in the preamble it looks harmless and simple enough on the face of it. It calls for

Marconi Wireless Company
the extension of Canadian patent No. 98083 granted on March 20, 1906, for certain new and useful improvements in instruments for converting alternating electric currents into continuous currents. The period of extension asked for is seven years. This patent involves, as my hon. friend (Mr. Marler) has said, the basic patent known as the Fleming valve or rectifier, on which all modem radio rests. This valve or rectifier was invented by Dr. Fleming of the University of London and was patented in England in 1904. The patent term in England was 14 years and expired in the year 1918. It was not renewed. This device was patented in the United States in 1906, the term there being seventeen years, and it was not renewed although application was made for an extension of time. The patent was taken out in Canada in 1906 and the term expired in March last. As my hon. friend has said, application was made in the dying days of last session to have the time extended.

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman
bear in mind the remarks I have made? The objections raised by the Senate are eliminated from the present bill.

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext:
It is true the objections
of the Senate have been eliminated from it, but those are not the objectionable features of the bill. At least, they are not really so objectionable in my opinion, whatever my hon. friend may think. My objection to the bill I is, in brief, that it will lay on the general public of Canada, particularly on radio enthusiasts, a very heavy financial burden. And I shall briefly indicate why. This patent is the device which I hold in my hand and which will be familiar to every radio user. It is the vacuum tube or Fleming valve or rectifier, and it consists essentially of two electrodes, a hot and a cold, within a vacuum. It was discovered by Edison before Dr. Fleming's time that a high voltage, high frequency alternating current will go only in one direction between a hot and a cold electrode, but this principle was made use of by Dr. Fleming and applied to wireless telegraphy. This device, with the addition of a third electrode, the grid, introduced by Dr. De Forest of New York, revolutionized wireless telegraphy and made possible modem wireless telephony or radio as we know it. If this bill passes, every j radio user in Canada will be affected because 1 if the extension of time is granted it will be of no advantage to the manufacturing company unless they put up the price of the tubes. This tube which I hold in my hand sold for $9 while the patent stood. A year
ago in February, just before the expiry of the patent, the price of the tube dropped to $6 and in February of this year it went down to $4. Someone suggests that it has, gone below that.

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext:
Since the patent ran
out?

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext: Yes, the year after it expired. Now, I venture the prediction that the price will be advanced at least $2 if not more if the patent is extended.

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman
look at section 2 of the bill? Does it not permit others to manufacture the same article in Canada provided manufacture is already started?

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext:
I have no information
that that has been done to any extent although I cannot speak with any certainty. I do not think that this device has been manufactured by anyone who will not be affected by the extension of the patent. Section 3 provides that the act shall not affect or restrict in any way the manufacture in Canada of an invention, covered by the said patent, for export out of Canada. The principle apparently seems to be to lay all the burden on the Canadian radio user. In the special copyright committee this afternoon Mr. Cartier who has charge of the broadcasting station of La Presse in Montreal was examined. He stated that there are 400,000 radio receiving stations in Canada, and he expressed the opinion that 100,000 at least of these are users of the tube set receiving apparatus, the others being users of the crystal set, who would not be affected. My estimate is that if there are 100,000 users of tube sets to-day there will be a million users of them in 1931 by the time the patent expires.

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that
these sets have all the way from two to five tubes?

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext: Yes, these tube sets may have as many as eight tubes, according to the results which the owner wishes to obtain. The life of these tubes is short, particularly in the hands of amateurs; they are being burned out and broken every day. I estimate conservatively that every radio user will require on an average at least two and a half tubes a year, probably more.

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext:
(York):	How much do
they cost?

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED

The type which I have
here costs $4. The price varies according to the variety. '

Marconi Wireless Company

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext: How much does an electric bulb cost?

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext: I do not know; the price of electric bulbs varies as well. But if the average owner of a radio set uses two and a half tubes a year, and my estimate of the number of owners of radio sets is anywhere near correct, the public of Canada during the next six years in which the patent would be extended under this bill, as one year has already expired, would use 7,500,000 tubes. If the price is advanced $2 per tube, this would involve an outlay on the part of the radio public of Canada of $15,000,000. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that would lay a heavier burden on the radio public of this country than the proposed Petersen bill would lay on the public generally. There is another point to be considered. If this patent is extended, there are innumerable patents covering improvements of this device, some of them mechanical, some of them electrical, and there is no reason why the holders of those patents should not come to this parliament and ask for extension also. For these reasons I submit that there is no justification for the extension of this particular patent. We have the reputation of being long-suffering, but I venture to say, Sir, that the House will not inflict this burden upon the long-suffering people of Canada.

maintopic: MARCONI WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I think the House and the country as a whole are to be congratulated on our having among us one with the technical knowledge of this subject which has been displayed by the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Wallace). Being a skilled electrical engineer, he was able to detect this seemingly innocent little bill as it was on its progress through the House. All civilized countries have patent and copyright acts; it is fitting that that should be so. The object is to protect an inventor or an author in his right to enjoy the product of his brain; and, speaking generally, for my part I would say that these rights should be primarily considered irrespective of the manufacturers' or the publishers' rights. Our patent act gives a man the right to his invention for a period of eighteen years. In the judgment of many that time is too long; certainly it is long enough. If the term is to be changed at all, I think we would favour reducing rather than lengthening it. Many reasons might be advanced why this patent should not be continued. The hon. member who has introduced the bill (Mr. Marler) has indicated certain reasons why in his judgment it should be continued. I suppose the same reasons

could be advanced by almost every patentee for similar indulgence. But this particular patent has run its course of eighteen years. It is now nearly eight years since the close of the war, and its holders have had an opportunity to enjoy the profits arising from the manufacture of the article covered by the patent. I can well imagine that no bill that might be proposed to the House this session would arouse such strong protests from the public of Canada generally as would this particular bill, and I venture to say that hon. members will hear very soon from a tremendous number of radio fans all through the country if the prayer of the bill is granted and the patent extended.
Motion (Mr. Marler) negatived.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
The point of importance is the fact that the House concurred in the reports and the reports contained the statements which I made to the House this afternoon.
At six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was directing the attention of the House to a series of communications to be found on the government files and which have been laid on the table of the House, communications which make it perfectly clear, I submit, that one interest after another in Canada was suggesting to the government of the day, of which my right hon. friend was the leader, that the high rates which were being charged on ocean freights were having the effect of destroying the export trade of the particular industries with which they were concerned, were in fact helping to bring about the closing of many of those industries and to increase unemployment in Canada. It was pointed out that the general effect was adverse to Canadian industries while helping to build up the industries of the United States, the railroads of the United States and transport from United States ports. In other words, the procedure of this ocean combine has been to establish rates, undoubtedly through the associations which these big interests enjoy among each other, from American ports to
Ocean Shipping Rates

European and British ports considerably lower than the rates fixed from Canadian ports to British ports. The result has been that our Canadian industries, owing to the higher rate of transport across the Atlantic to European and British ports, find themselves unable to compete with similar industries in the United States and, what is even worse, find that the higher rates from Canadian ports to British ports are causing much of the raw material of Canada to go to the United States to be manufactured there, thus building up United States industries at the expense of Canadian industries and stimulating the shipments of goods to European countries through United States ports instead of through our own ports. One instance that I spoke of as attracting a good deal of attention was that of the milling industry. Representations were made over and over again to the government of my right hon. friend opposite by this industry in Canada that owing to the fixing by the combine of lower rates upon flour from the United States to British and continental ports than from Canadian ports to the same point overseas, a large volume of grain was going from Canada into the United States to be ground in American mills, while our own mills, unable to export any flour, were closing their doors. What was true in the case of the flour and milling industry, according to the representations I have been reading to the House, has been true also with respect to the cattle trade and, according to representations which I shall read, has been true also with respect to many other industries. I was speaking of the clothes peg industry before the House rose; I mentioned it because it is one of numerous industries affected. What I have said is true also of the dairying industry, of the fruit growing industry, of the canning industry, and of others of great variety and scope. Hon. gentlemen opposite speak about raising the tariff wall, about putting a ring around Canada to prevent the competition of American goods, yet they are prepared to permit these ocean rates to be so regulated by a combine that our raw material is being drained from Canada to build up industries in the United States which compete with ours in export trade, a regulation of rates moreover which makes it impossible for our industries to ship goods from Canadian ports to Great Britain and European ports in competition with shipments going from American ports.
Now may I continue reading some of these representations?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Will the right hon. gentleman permit me a question? Do the tramps on the Atlantic take flour? I understood that

flour was one of the commodities in competition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
With regard to tramps I shall have a word to say later. As I understand it, tramp steamers are ever on the lookout for business, picking it up whereever they can can. But when you study the rates they have been receiving, you find that they are just a little bit below the rates which the combine fixes. In other words, the rates the tramp steamers get ,are based upon the rate which the combine originally fixes. If the combine's rate is high, the tramp steamer will be getting a very high rate, even though it is a little lower than that of the combine. On the other hand if the rates are kept down by the conference the tramp steamer will fix a slightly lower rate. Sc that so far as I can make out, the rates which the tramp steamers get are in the first instance based upon the rates fixed by the combine for the liners.
Now, may I read further regarding these ocean freight rates on flour? I have before me a letter which will illustrate what I have just said. It is from the Dominion Millers' Association to the then Prime Minister, the present leader of the opposition, and is as follows:
1801 Royal Bank Building,
Toronto, January 15, 1921.
Re: Ocean Freight Rates on Flour Hon. Arthur Meighen,
Prime Minister,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-You will remember when Mr. Gear and his colleagues appeared before you and the other members of the cabinet on the above question that he stated in reply to Sir Henry Drayton's query as to the freight rates being fixed in New York for the Canadian lines that they always took care to protect the interests of the Canadian shippers.
In the latter part of December the rate on wheat dropped from 40c. to 25c. per 100 lbs. and under the order of the U.S. Shipping Board, the rates on vessels subject to that board dropped on flour to 30c. per 100 lbs. making the differential 5c. per 100 lbs. as before.
Application was made to the Canadian shipping companies to reduce their rates likewise to 30c. per 100 lbs. on flour but we are informed that at a meeting of the steamship agents it was decided not to make any reduction with the result that the Canadian millers are now to pay 45c. per 100 lbs. by the Canadian steamship agents while U.S. millers or for that matter Canadians, can ship flour at 30c. per 100 lbs. via New York, Baltimore, etc.
I wanted to be positive of this before taking the matter up with you and to-day saw a letter from New York quoting 30 cents rate on flour to U.K. ports for January shipment while 45 cents has been the lowest rate offered from Canada although we understand we can get it for 25 cents to continental ports.
It seems a remarkable situation that Canadian government steamers should refuse to carry flour from Canadian ports at the same rate as U.S. government steamers will carry flour for both U.S. and Canadian millers from U.S. ports thus discriminating against Canadian ports and Canadian railways and compelling

Ocean Shipping Rates
Canadian millers to ship via U.S. railroads through U.S. ports.
This is especially extraordinary at the present time when unemployment is so great in Canada and also in view of the fact that it w-as reported in the press, one of the government steamers has been chartered to load in New York for some foreign port.
We sincerely trust that you will take this matter up immediately and take whatever steps are necessary to secure the 30 cent rate on flour from Canadian ports as well as U.S. ports. It looks very peculiar and bears strong evidence of there being a combine in ocean freight rates the U.K. when freight can be secured at 25 cents to the continent from the same agents as ask 45 cents to the U.K. ports.
Whilst speaking of flour, I might quote two other letters, one from the Fischer Flour Mills, of Pembroke, Ontario, dated April 4, 1921, addressed to the Department of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa, and reading as follows:
Re: Flour Shipments to Danzig
Gentlemen,-We have recently been submitting offers for carload shipments of flour to the Danzig (Free State) authorities and would have secured handsome contract if it had not been for the transportation charges which appear to be considerably higher from Canada to Danzig than New York to Danzig, and it is only on account of the saving in freight the New York interests secured the order.
We have been promised an order on the basis of equal freight. Is it not possible for us to secure part of this business and can you not please find out for us what would be the cheapest way to ship flour from Pembroke to the port of Danzig. Of course, so far we had to figure on St. John, N.B., freight which will be considerably reduced as soon as we could ship from Montreal.
We will be very much indebted to you for assisting us in this proposition. Business is slack and it would seem a pity if orders for flour which are so badly needed here should be all going to the American competition.
Trusting to receive full information at an early date, we remain,
Faithfully yours,
Fischer Flour Mills.
Then on April 8, 1921, the same firm writing to the Commercial Intelligence branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and referring to this file, says:
Dear Sirs,-We are very much indebted to you for 3'our kind letter of the 6th inst. in connection with ocean freight rates on flour to Danzig, Europe.
We have informed you that it costs $4.00 to $5.00 to ship one ton of flour from New York to Danzig, and we are to-day advised by the C.P.R. that their rate from Montreal to Danzig is 48 cents a hundred or $9.60 a ton.
In other words, under the arrangement which this combine worked out, flour was going from New York to Danzig at from $4 to $5 per ton, whereas the rate from Montreal was $9.60 per ton. This firm adds:
This is a remarkable difference and as you will readily see, will surely kill the trade for Canadian maufacturers desirous of exporting to the above port.
Your co-operation is indeed highly appreciated and we are looking forward to encouraging news.
Faithfully yours,
Fischer Flour Mills.
I wish again to direct the attention of the House to the phraseology used by these various shippers. One after the other refers to the circumstance, not that his industry is being prejudiced, not that his industry is being impaired, but that it is being killed or destroyed. "This is a remarkable difference," this firm Says, "and as you will readily see, will surely kill the trade for Canadian manufacturers." So much for representations with respect to the shipments of flour.
Now let me give a quotation or two with regard to canned goods. There is another large industry in this country, which affects market gardeners as well. This is a communication dated Hamilton, January 24, 1921, from the Dominion Canners, Limited, addressed to the Department of Trade and Commerce, Ottaw-a:
Dear Sir,-We have reliable information that freight ra es on canned goods from San Francisco to U.K. ports have been fixed at $1.10 per 100 lbs. or the same rate as from Atlantic ports, provided the goods are not strapped.
You will readily appreciate that it is impossible for us to compete with California packers on this freight basis. The rates of freight now being asked by the various steamship companies, owing to their pool arrangements, is altogether too high and while the outlook for business under the most favourable conditions is not encouraging, the high freight rates are completely killing it.
There again is the same expression as was used in a previous letter, "the high freight rates are completely killing it," namely, the export business in canned goods in this country. The letter continues:
It should be in the Canadian interests to see that the freight ra'es established from Canadian ports to Great Britain are in line with the California rates. You understand, of course, that in California they are able to pack very much cheaper than We are in eastern Canada, owing to the tremendous business which they do there and owing to the large quantities of fruits and vegetables grown especially for canning factories on a very large scale. If there is any possibility of reducing rates, we belive it is in the best interests of all concerned.
If our information is correct, many boats are tied up for lack of freight and the holding of freights at prohibitive prices is only resulting in the goods not moving at all.
Yours very truly,
Dominion Canners Limited.
The next is a communication with respect to rolled oats, another industry of importance in this country. I shall read only one or two paragraphs. This letter is addressed to the Right Hon. Sir George E. Foster, Minister of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa, and is from the Dominion Millers' Association:
Hon. Sir.-I am asked to call your attention to the high ocean freight on rolled oats.
Then this paragraph appears:
The oatmeal mills have found it impossible to sell any oatmeal for export in the face of these pro-
Ocean Shipping Rates

hibitive ocean freight rates with the result that the Canadian oatmeal mills are shut down while the Old Country mills are busy and the steamship companies are not getting the oatmeal to carry and ships including those of the Canadian Marine, are lying idle for days at a time in port waiting for sufficient cargo to accumulate to justify their sailing.
The last paragraph reads:
You will of course realize that the fact that oatmeal mills are shut down has an adverse effect on the price of oats as it takes ten bushels of oats to make one barrel of oatmeal so if the steamship companies would reduce their freight to a workable basis, it would not only be a benefit to the steamship companies themselves, and the milling industry but also to the farming community.
1 have the honour to be,
Your obedient servant,
C. B. Watts,
Secretary.

What is the date
of that letter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
The letter is
dated March 16, 1921. I am reading representations which my right hon. friend and his government had before them with respect to these high ocean rates, and the point I wish to draw to the attention of the House in that connection is that this problem is by no means a new one. It is not a matter with which the Preston report is concerned one way or the other. I am trying to show that the government departments are full of these representations from all the leading industries of our country, and it is on the representations which have been made to the government, independent altogether of any report made by Mr. Preston, that the government action in this present connection is based. I wish also to make this e'lear, that this condition is just as bad-I should n.ot say as bad, it is worse to-day, because the rates that are complained of here have been increased since that time on all the commodities to which I have made reference, and there is no guarantee whatever that next month unless the government steps in and takes action such as we are taking to-day, the rates may not be raised again. There is no control whatever. This combine regulates the rates any way they please, and every industry of anjr importance in this country is pointing out to the government that its export trade is being thwarted, if not destroyed entirely, by the high ocean rates; and in addition to that 'businesses are being closed down and men are being thrown out of employment. If my right hon. friend wants to know why men are out of employment and why businesses are closing down, he will find it in these representations which have been made to the government as to the impossibility of shipping goods abroad at the high rates 
which are being charged by the working of this combine.
Now let me take another communication in regard to the rates on cattle. This is a communication addressed to Hon. Dr. S. F. Tolmie, Minister of Agriculture, dated August 1, 1921, from the Stock Growers' Protective Association of Western Canada, Calgary, Alta., and signed by W. F. Stevens, secretary. Hon. gentlemen opposite wall know whether that association has a right to speak on behalf of those for whom it professes to speak in this communication:
Dear Sir-I am taking the liberty of directing your attention to the severe drop in market prices for cattle. According to a report just received from the commission firms in Calgary, $5.25 per hundredweight is at the present time the top price for butcher steers. Something is necessary to be done or the live stock business of production in western Canada will be reduced to a lower level than has been the case for many years. I have been requested by the directors to communicate with you in this respect and direct your attention to the present situation.
I have been asked to acknowledge our appreciation of the reduction that has been made in the price of steamship space, and also to say that another similar reduction will have to be made if our stock growers are to receive for their cattle a price which even approximates the cost of production.
I feel free in bringing this matter to your attention because I know you fully understand western Canadian conditions and the importance of the live stock industry to the three prairie provinces.
I trust that you will be able to secure in the near future another reduction in the price of ocean space.
Thanking you in anticipation, I am,
Yours very truly,
W. JF. Stevens,
Secretary.
These are communications wThich have been laid on the table of the House. I wish to quote from two or three more, simply to dispel from the minds of hon. members and the public once and for all, that the representations in Mr. Preston's report are the only ones that the government has had before it in this matter. These further representations to which I wish to refer were made long before Mr. Preston was asked to have anything to do with the subject, and are wholly independent of anything to which his report relates.
Another of the industries with regard to which communications have been received relating to ocean rates is the corn broom industry. Meakins & Sons, Limited, Hamilton, sent a communication, dated December 9, 1919, in which they said that a dozen corn brooms shipped by the Head line to Dublin from Montreal cost them eleven shillings ocean freight, while a dozen of the same brooms shipped by the Head line from Baltimore to Dublin or Belfast costs them from five shillings and four pence for the

Ocean Shipping Rates
small grades to seven shillings and eight pence for the very largest corn broom. They would average about six shillings and six pence per dozen. The communication goes on to say.
The difference between six shillings and six pence per dozen and an average of eleven shillings is such a great difference that there is absolutely no chance for us to compete, although these goods are in great demand both in Ireland and Scotland, and we know that we can manufacture them as cheap here as they can be manufactured in the United States.
The writer goes on to remark:
It seems too bad to see this trade lost to us, more especially when the same line of steamers carries the goods from West St. John to Ireland as carries the goods from Baltimore to Ireland. Cannot something be done in the matter?
We remain,
Yours truly,
Meakins & Sons Limited,
W. J. Meakins.
Thus it is seen that the very same ship3 carrying commodities from Canadian and American ports charge a very much higher rate from Canadian ports to Ireland than from American ports.
Here is another communication from the Sutherland Innes Company Limited with respect to the cooperage industry, dated Chatham, Ontario, January 24, 1919. It is addressed to Mr. O'Hara, Department of Trade and Commerce, and deals with the shipment of cooperage stock to Great Britain. The general manager says in part, I will not quote the whole letter:
It looks to me like a deliberate attempt-perhaps made through ignorance but very likely through greed
to destroy the trade in cooperage from Canada to Great Britain.
I think this is a matter for your department to take up, as it certainly is not reasonable, at the present time, with all the ships that are going from St. John and Halifax, to extort a rate of $3 per hundrrd pounds on cooperage stock, when previous to the war, steamers were rigorously soliciting the same business, at from 17 cents to 35 cents per hundred pounds according to the season.
There is an increase in ocean rates if you like, an increase from 17 to 35 cents per hundred pounds to $3 per hundred pounds. These are the high ocean rates of which manufacturing concerns in this country, as well as agriculture and other industries are complaining. The manager of this concern encloses a statement from a representative setting out these facts more in detail.
