speechtext:
Yes, I have some late ones and I will bring them along in a moment. Then there is a communication with respect to pig iron from Fraser, Brace & Company, Limited, S3 Craig Street West, Montreal, dated April 17, 1919 to the Department of Trade and Commerce, which states:
We manufacture pig iron in electric furnaces at Shawinigan Falls and at present have a representative in England who writes that he can secure orders for from 500 to 1,000 tons per month over the balance of the year. However, we find it impossible to get a freight rate. The White Star line and Robert Reford Company, practically refuse to quote. Can you give us any assistance in this matter? We are asked to quote on this business c.i.f. London, Antwerp, Northern French ports, Genoa and Italy.
Your assistance will be appreciated. The Canadian Pacific O.S. have just quoted rate $25 a gross ton London subject to tonnage and change without notice.
Here is another important Canadian industry, the lumber industry. A firm in the Old Country acting as agents for Canadian concerns, Spence, Lock & Company communicated as follows with the High Commissioner at London, and the letter was sent out for the department here to deal with.
I will only read a sufficient number of paragraphs from the letter to illustrate its tenor:
27 Clements Lane
Lombard Street,
London, E.C. 4,
7th, September, 1921.
His Excellency
The High Commissioner for Canada.
The object of this letter is to bring before your notice the urg. nt necessity of lower lumber freights from Canada to this country.
Our interest in the matter is that of selling agents for many large* Canadian houses. From the resultant confusion-
He is speaking of the war-
-we are only just emerging; during the past few weeks something like a recognized free on board value is gradually shaping, and there has even been a slight firming up of prices. A good deal of business has been done and more confidence is felt.
If, however, we turn to the sources of what has been sold we find that Finland has provided most of it, that Sweden has sold a fair quantity, and that Canada has literally sold nothing.
From eastern Canada we look normally for large supplies of spruce, but this year buyers have taken European white in preference as they find it not only in the main better, but actually much cheaper.
Canadian freights are bout 100/- as against about 50/- from Sweden and Finland. That is the first reason. The second is that the Finnish exchange is so low they can afford to sell at prices which appear ruinous to the Swede, and quite impossible to the Canadian.
The only hope we see for an awakening of spruce business is in a determination by sellers to accept the facts of the situation by a bold cut simultaneously with a sensible reduction in the freight rate. If freights could be set at 60/- that would give sellers
Ocean Shipping Rates

about $34 and $22 per thousand feet f.o.b. We think that at such rates a sound and steady business could be gradually worked up again, and we do not doubt that sellers could be eventually induced to accept business on such terms.
We ask your pardon for addressing you at this length but the matter seems to us of considerable importance, and we would venture to beg your assistance in bringing your influence to bear to ameliorate the position as regards the freight.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
The letter is dated 7 September 1921. I have another communication from Huntsville, Ontario, dated August 22, 1921. This letter is from the Anglo Canadian Leather Company, Limited. It was evidently sent by this company 9 p.m. to the then member for the constituency who apparently forwarded it to the Minister of Trade and Commerce because it appears on the files of the department:
Dr. Peter McGibbon, M.C., M.P.,
Bracebridge, Ontario.
Dear Dr. McGibbon,-We write to you to enlist your good offices to assist us in an effort which we are making to obtain a reduction in the ocean freight rate on sole leather from Montreal to England.
The present rate of $2 per hundred pounds is eight times the pre-war rate. As late as 1919 we shipped large quantities of sole leather at $1.25 per hundred pounds-or five times the pre-war rate.
We understand on very reliable authority that the general average of cargoes are being shipped at less than three times pre-war rate. Dry hides are being shipped at $1 per hundred pounds, from South America, against a pre-war rate of 80 cents per hundred pounds.
From this you will see that the rate on sole leather is unjust and entirely out of line with general rates. We have been endeavouring to induce the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited, Montreal, to authorize a rate of 75 cents or three times the prewar rate, but without success.
We understand that the shipping business is exceedingly quiet and we constantly see references in the press to the effect that government ships are idle and that they are endeavouring to open up a new channel of trade to keep them busy, etc., it seems to us that if they would endeavour to keep alive some of the old trade that existed before the war it would be the proper way to go about an increase of business. The rate of $2 per hundred pounds practically shuts us off from export business in sole leather-
Another export business shut off.
[DOT]-as this business is done on a very close margin of profit.
Then he goes on to say:
In fact for many years before the war we suppose that we did not make more than a cent a pound on our export business. You will understand from this how impossible it is to compete with the English tanners when a $2 freight rate has to be figured in the price.
You have evidence both in Huntsville and Brace-bridge of the condition of our industry at the present

time. Our Bracebridge plant is almost entirely shut down and while we are doing a little more at Huntsville just now, we have been idle all summer. Normally 50 per cent of our output goes abroad and there is no chance whatever to operate our plants to capacity or anywhere near it, until we are able to export freely. You will see from this the necessity of having a freight rate upon which business can be done.
We have no doubt you will realize also from what we have said the vital importance of this whole matter. It means something to every working man and merchant in the towns of Huntsville and Brace-bridge.
Thanking you for your help in the past and for anything you may be able to do for us in the present case, we are,
Yours respectfully,
Anglo Canadian Leather Company, Ltd., Chas. G. Shaw.
I think I have quoted from enough communications to bear out the truth of the statement that I have made, that in a great variety of the industries of this country, industries upon which communities largely depend for their livelihood and which are therefore really all-important in the country's economic life, the export trade has been, if not completely, at any rate very largely destroyed, with the result that industry after industry has had to close down and unemployment has increased in the different communities.

speechtext: No, some of them are prior to that and they come down to 1921. The quotations I have made have been in order to show that hon. gentlemen opposite had plenty of representations made to them on this score. They know very well the source of unemployment and the cause of the closing down of industries, if such be the case, but they are failing to recognize, or at least to admit the right cause. They are endeavouring to have it appear that the tariff is in some way responsible for the closing down of these different industries, while they are being told, according to the representations made by the heads of the industries themselves that it is the high ocean rates that make it impossible for export trade to be carried on.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Will the Prime Minister tell us how it happens that under this terrible handicap of high freight rates, our export trade is *1,045,351,056, and the favourable balance of trade since last year has increased *280,000,000?

Ocean Shipping Rates

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
That is in spite of the situation that I have been describing. It would be very much greater if this handicap were removed. If the bon. member will study the figures, he will find that that gain has been confined largely to very considerable exports in two or three particular lines, but that others have suffered.
May I come to some of the representations that were made to the present government? The present government like the previous government had direct representations made to it, for example, with respect to the differential on flour from American ports as against Canadian ports. A communication which I received from the secretary, Mr. Watts, on January 11, 1922, begins as follows:
Re high ocean freight rates. As the United States' millers only pay nineteen cents per 100 pounds in United States' funds while the Canadian millers have to pay twenty-four cents per 100 pounds In Canadian funds on flour to Great .Britain, I am taking the liberty of sending you a copy of the representations made to the late Prime Minister and his colleagues on this question last August as I expect the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be bringing this question to your attention shortly if he has not already done so.
In another communication, dated January 21, 1922, Mr. Watts states as follows:
This is a matter of vital importance, not only to the milling industry, .but also to the transportation and agricultural interests in Canada, as at the present time Canadian wheat can be ground in American mills and shipped to Great Britain at nineteen cents per one hundred pounds while Canadian flour, even shipped in Canadian government boots, has to pay twenty -four cents per one hundred pounds. This means also a serious loss to Canadian labour, not only those employed in the mills, but in the transportation of the products as well. For these reasons, we sincerely trust you will be able to ibe present at the meeting and give us your aid in having flour milled in Canada, carried at the same rates of freight to the United Kingdom as flour milled in the United States.
I could mention other communications from the same association, but I can say in a word that they repeat in large part what is there stated. The government undertook at once to make representations on this matter, without very considerable success at the beginning. On July 10, 1923, this communication was received, and it shows how serious the matter had become at that time:
The rate on Canadian boats from Montreal is 19 cents per 100 pounds, so the fact that there is a combine among the boats trading from Canada and that the Canada Steamship Lines has protested to New York against Canadian flour being carried from the United States ports at the same rate as United States flour, and insisting that it 'be carried at the same rate as the boats sailing from the Canadian ports were charging, as brought out before the investigation Jby the special agricultural committee, had no effect.
The Ontario mills still continue to go to the wall, and if this discrimination continues long enough there

will be few mills left in Ontario excepting those located at lake ports where they can get the benefit of the all water rates, or competitive rates based on the all water.
Yours truly,	.
C. B. Watts.
That was a serious statement-"The Ontario mills still continue to go to the wall." On August 16, 1923, the following communication was sent also by Mr. Watts to Mr. Robb, at that time Minister of Trade and Commerce, re high ocean freight rates:
In further reference to our letter of yesterday re the above, we beg to advise you that we are to-day offered a rate of 12h cents per 100 pounds on A-l steamers on flour from New York to Hamburg, last half of August or first half of September.
The rate from Montreal to Hamburg is 19 cents or 61 cents per 100 pounds or 13 cents per barrel higher than the rate via New York.
Then omitting a paragraph and coming to the concluding paragraph:
The mills in Ontario have gone out of business during the past year or two at an appalling rate and if this discrimination continues, it will only be a short time before the milling industry in Ontario is wiped out excepting a few mills -that are financially strong enough to work at a loss for possibly a year or two longer when the few that survive will probably be able to charge such prices as will well repay them for the lean years they have passed through, but it will not bring into existence again the large number of mills which that unfair discriminatory freight rates have ruined and driven out of existence.
Those representations are very similar to the representations which were made to the government of my right hon. friend opposite. I am happy to say that the present government have been able to do something in this matter; that they have been able, through the representations they have made, to get the same rate on flour from Canadian ports as from United States' ports, and that the situation has been remedied, at least for the present. The government took up the matter repeatedly with the shipping companies through the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the present Acting Minister of Finance, (Mr. Robb), and the present minister, it was also taken up at the Imperial conference by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) and the ex-Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin). It was brought before the Imperial Shipping committee and stressed very strongly; it was kept before them by the present High Commissioner in England. They were asked to continue their investigations here and they did so, with the result that they have secured an understanding from the combine that the rates on flour from Canadian ports will not exceed the rates from American ports. So that the situation has been remedied to that extent. But as matters stand there is no guarantee other than the word of there com-

Ocean Shipping Rates

panies that these rates will be maintained. I would point out that while that result has been achieved in regard to one commodity, flour, these preferentials favouring American ports to the exclusion of Canadian ports remain in large measure what they have been with respect to other commodities. Unless some step is taken such as that which the government proposes in the legislation about to be brought down, it is difficult to see how the situation can be remedied at all.
I have here a communication with regard to cattle. It is of recent date and shows that these representations still have force and that they relate to present conditions.

speechtext:
The report was laid on the table of the Ontario House just a few days ago, and this summary, I understand, was released to the press on February 24, this year. I have tried to get a copy of the report itself, but I am advised that it will not be printed for another day or two. Now for the quotation:
Ocean rates hold down export trade to Britain. It is true that 1924 shows the largest shipping of any year since the embargo was removed, running 80,000 head. But it obvious that Ontario alone is capable of producing beef cattle in volume far exceeding the present export trade. A special bulletin of the Dominion Department of Agriculture in 1923 welcomec' removal of the embargo as a new order of things warranting official experiments in the shipment of steers to England. The experiments were intended to demonstrate to cattle raisers that live cattle realize considerably higher returns than chilled beef shipments. This committee has followed shipments from western Ontario to England conducted by men experienced in the cattle trade and the results showed that as many were unprofitable as profitable. One of the first witnesses before this committee said: "I am the only farmer in a ten-mile area who has cattle for export in his barn. I have 95 acres and from 50 to 55 cattle. There are a hundred others at least who could feed and accommodate as many in the section. They have the barns. But they do not enter the trade because there is no profit in it. Ontario should be able to ship as many live cattle to England as does Ireland. It would mean prosperity to the province. The market is in England for as many as we can send, no matter what they say about the dead meat trade. The business does not prosper because it is without the attraction of profit.''
The potential power of Ontario to engage in the movement of live cattle to Britain cannot be fully developed because of existing influences. Mr. Shamberg of New York is the chief buyer for export. Mr. Shamberg's agents are in the Union Stock Yards, Toronto; in the office of the International Mercantile Marine at No. 1 Broadway, New York, and at the British ports. The committee satisfied itself that the usefulness of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine is limited by the North Atlantic freight conference. It came to the conclusion that with his widespread power and influence Mr. Shamberg controls the profits of Ontario cattle raisers. He has inside information at all times by reason of which he can cancel optioned spaces or send his own cattle according to the trend of the market. The less optimistic in Ontario have been driven out and the industry is not what it should be.
Correspondence with the Dominion government in August last is quoted and the report goes on to say, "Inasmuch as definite action by the Dominion government was thus implied, the committee thought it inadvisable to carry investigation further. The committee recommends that the Ontario government strongly urge upon the Dominion government full consideration of the interests and requirements of Ontario shippers in whatever federal policy may be decided upon to secure reduction of ocean rates."

Now I come to what seems to me, Mr. Speaker, the crux of the whole situation. It

will be argued that ocean rates have risen in consequence of the increased cost of ocean transportation, and of conditions as they have been since the war. No one will deny that it was to be expected that ocean rates would rise somewhat, but I would point out that everything that can be said with respect to the increase of rates on the ocean can be said with equal, or greater force with respect to the increase of rates by rail, and the essential feature which this House should consider is whether the increases in ocean rates are fair as compared with the increases in rates by rail. In the one case, in railway rates, you have a controlled situation. You have a railway commission that has control of railway rates; it controls the rates, having regard to the return on capital invested, having regard to the wages that are being paid to labour, and having regard to the interests of the travelling and shipping public. But so far as ocean rates are concerned, there is no control save that which is exercised by this conference itself; there is no control on the part of the public, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if it is discovered that ocean rates by comparison are out of all proportion wTith the increases that have taken place on the railways, this government has established to the full a case demanding the immediate attention of this House by way of legislation to effectively reduce ocean rates.

I will answer that by saying that the government in fixing ocean rates will endeavour to have regard to the rates charged on the railways, where regard is being had to the factors to which my hon. friend has alluded.
May I point out at once that so far as this discussion is concerned, it is really immaterial whether a combine exists or does not exist. May I say to the House, as I mentioned to my hon. friend the other night, that I believe in these days of world competition large organization of industry is essential, and something in the nature of combined effort; but just because I believe it is necessary, just because 1 believe it-is certain to come, I believe the more strongly in the necessity of some control over these all powerful organizations; and that is the situation which is presenting itself on the Atlantic ocean at the present time. These companies are left to themselves to make arrangements as to steamship rates. In making those arrangements, if one judges by the rates that are quoted, it would appear that the public interest is not considered to anything like the extent of the interest of the other parties involved in the transaction. In a word, to carry on industry, capital is necessary, labour is necessary, management is necessary, and the public, as a consuming and producing entity, is also a necessary factor. All four are entitled to due consideration. I think the facts will show that so far as ocean rates are concerned, the public, if it has been considered at all, has been considered in a very remote way.
I have in my hand two receipts that speak for themselves. They were sent to me by an agent of steamship and railway lines in an Ontario constituency. They are two receipts that were in his possession which disclose the rates charged on the ocean and by rail on immigrants coming from Great Britain to Canada. The receipt of April 1, 1914, shows the third class ocean fare for one person as $32.50, and the Canadian railway fare from the port of landing to a locality in the constituency mentioned as $8.70. The other receipt is dated April 19, 1924, ten years later. It shows the third class steamship rate as $75, or an increase of 130 per cent over the rate in 1914, and the railway rate for the same distance is $15.70, or an increase of 81 per cent. In other words, the ocean rate, judging by these two receipts, had increased by 130 per cent, while the railway rate, for the same distance, had increased by only 81 per cent. Now will anyone say for a moment that the railways have net been subjected to just as important consideration in the matter
of their rates as ocean transports? As a matter of fact, ocean rates for labour have not gone up as much as rates for labour on the railways. The railways have to look after the maintenance of roadbed, a costly business; there is no roadbed maintenance in the case of steamship companies. Great stress has been laid on the fact that immigrants are treated muoh more comfortably on the steamships to-day; but the same may be said of their treatment by the railways. Take, for instance, the expenditure on railway stations, and the accommodation provided for immigrants at the ports of landing on colonist sleepers and the like. The railway accommodation is very much better to-day than it was ten years ago. In all of these particulars I think it can be urged wfith fairness that the railways have been subjected to just as much in the way of increased cost as the steamship companies; and yet when you come to look at the charges you find that the increase in ocean rates is infinitely higher than the increase in railway rates.

speechtext: What about the accommodation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WAGE INCREASES PAID BY RAILWAYS COMPARED WITH OCEAN CARRIERS
speechtext:
The improvement in accommodation during that time, if not greater, has been quite as great on the railways as it has been on the steamships. I wish to direct the attention of the House particularly to these figures because they illustrate in a concrete and simple way the difference between the controlled rates on land and the uncontrolled rates on the ocean. In the case of first class passengers in ten years there has been an increase in the rates charged, of 27 per cent on land, and of 129 per cent on sea. In the case of immigrants the increase amounts to 39 per cent on land and 168 per cent on the ocean. In view of figures of such a character, which cannot be disputed, I submit that the ocean rates, uncontrolled as they are, show a vast disparity as compared with the railway rates, and the obvious necessity of controlling the ocean rates becomes apparent the minute these figures are considered. I had intended to say
something further about the immigration rates but I will spare the House any further details on that score at the moment. Let me hasten to a conclusion in -what
10 p.m. I wish further to bring out. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that apart altogether from any representations that have been made in any report by Mr. Preston, a comparison of the railway rates to-day with ocean rates will show a vast increase in the percentage of increase on the ocean as compared with the increase that has taken place on the land, and hence the necessity for some speedy method of effective control of ocean rates is obvious.
As regards the question of a method of ocean control, only two or three alternatives present themselves. One is that the government itself should seek to build its own merchant marine and enter into competition with this vast and powerful combine. Another is that the government should endeavour to bring about some form of control by a commission. The third is that the government should take some such step as that which we are taking at the present time of making an arrangement with a private company of giving them in return for receiving the right to control the rates a fair consideration. Apart from those three, nothing remains other than to let matters stand as they are.
Just a word with respect to each one of these three in turn. As to the government undertaking to build additional ships to compete with the combine itself, that matter was gone into very fully the other evening by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), who pointed out that if a step of that kind was to be taken, the time to have taken it was when the government was building a merchant marine, when it had ships ready to launch and was in a position to make these ships suitable for this particular trade. Members have asked:	Why cannot the present
merchant marine be used for the purpose? The answer is that ships of the merchant marine capable of handling the north Atlantic trade are few in number and are already employed on other routes in accordance with treaties that have been arrived at between different countries and Canada or are employed in large part on the Pacific ocean, in response to public need between Pacific ports and Australia and New Zealand, and are the only .profitable part of the merchant marine ships at the present time. I do not think this House would feel that the government would be justified in taking out of the merchant marine at this time, when the deficits of the merchant marine are what they are, the few
Ocean Shipping Plates

ships that are really proving an investment and putting them on the Atlantic route to fight the combine. I think it can be shown that in order effectively to combat a combine, such as exists on the Atlantic ocean, it is essential, whatever steamship line undertakes, the work, that it should have facilities in Europe and the Old Countiy as well as in this country.
*An hon. MEMBER :	Why is it that the
Canadian Government Merchant Marine have been losing so much money when they were charging the exorbitant rates that are being charged by the combine? Is there any definite reason for that?

speechtext: I cannot tell my hon. friend the reason for that excepting that there was a differential, discriminating against Canadian ports and possibly the rates may have been so high that they were not getting any business. That is one reason and I think it is a very sound reason.

speechtext: Will the Prime Minister explain why they were in the combine at all?

I presume that all such companies have their associations in matters of business and that the Canadian National Railways probably felt that if they were to get business at all through this merchant marine associated with them, it was necessary that they should fall into line with the other ships on the Atlantic or be boycotted by the conference. That is my understanding of the situation. Had they been boycotted, probably the position of the merchant marine would have been worse than it is at the present time.

speechtext: My hon. friend has put his finger on the right spot. As regards these ten ships, it is up to Sir William Petersen to demonstrate how he can do that. He contends that he is fortunately in a position, through his knowledge of shipping conditions and through his associations and the interests he has, to enter into this fight if he gets the backing which he is getting at the present time. He has-and this brings out the very point which I was trying to bring out a moment ago-docks of his own in the Old Country, docks which he controls. He has relations with business interests there and other shipping interests which he himself controls to enable him to carry on, as he believes, this fight successfully. He can do it in a manner in which the government merchant marine could not begin to do it. This government owns nothing in the way of docking facilities in Great Britain or Europe. It has not the associations which Sir William Petersen's company has. He is prepared to enter into this fight. It remains to be seen whether he will be successful or not.

The merchant marine is costing this country some eight million dollars in deficits. Would this House

maintopic: WAGE INCREASES PAID BY RAILWAYS COMPARED WITH OCEAN CARRIERS
speechtext: No, there were no limitations at all in the offer that was made. I do not wish to take up further time in discussing the merchant marine. As I say, that phase was gone into very fully by the Minister of Railways and Canals the other evening.

maintopic: WAGE INCREASES PAID BY RAILWAYS COMPARED WITH OCEAN CARRIERS
speechtext:
Has the
combine taken any step or steps in any way to cripple the merchant marine since it was taken out of the combine?

maintopic: WAGE INCREASES PAID BY RAILWAYS COMPARED WITH OCEAN CARRIERS
speechtext:
I have not heard of that, and I would be surprised if they had. Let me add this fact that one of the clauses in the contract with Sir William Petersen is that these ships which he is putting on the Atlantic are to work in conjunction with the Canadian National Railways and with the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. The probabilities are that, through co-operation in that regard, it may be possible to utilize even the merchant marine ships to greater advantage than it has been possible to do thus far.
Another alternative to the use of the government merchant marine is the one suggested in the amendment, namely control by a commission.
I need not emphasize the fact that commission control, so far as this country alone is concerned, is not a factor that can be considered; any control to be at all effective would have to be by means of international co-operation. The hon. gentleman suggests in his amendment that the different parts of the empire should unite to form a commission to control rates. Let us hope that this step will be taken; but thus far nothing has appeared to lead us to believe that the self governing Dominions and Great Britain are likely to come together in an effective way without a good deal of public opinion being aroused in the first instance; without some demonstration to bring matters nearer home than heretofore has been the case. Moreover, it is certain that a very considerable period would elapse before such a step could be taken. As was pointed out by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) the matter was brought to the attention of the British government in Sir Wilfrid Laurier's day; it was brought to the attention of the British authorities by a communication prepared by the then chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, the late Mr. Justice Mabee. But there was nothing effective accomplished in consequence, as the correspondence shows. I referred this afternoon to the visit to Great Britain of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) as chairman at that time of the railway commission, with the same end in view. And other correspondence has gone to show that over and over again efforts have been made to have the Imperial Shipping committee take some action; up to the present time those efforts have failed. Is it likely therefore that any step will be taken without in the first instance some action such as is now proposed to give a lead in the matter?

speechtext: Yes; this government had a sub-committee of the Imperial Shipping committee working on flour rates, and at the present time on our representation the committee is working on insurance. speechtext: When was this?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WAGE INCREASES PAID BY RAILWAYS COMPARED WITH OCEAN CARRIERS
speechtext:
The communication which was addressed to the British government in Sir Wilfrid Laurier's day. That should be sufficient to show that the matter has been before Great Britain for some time at least- Now, as I say, the alternatives are as between the government undertaking its own work of building ships, or relying upon this vague and remote control of an empire conference, whieh has been suggested in the amendment of my hon. friend; or, finally, taking some such step as the one now proposed, of giving a subsidy to a line which is prepared to put a certain number of ships in operation and give to the government the right of fixing rates.
Let me point out historically the steps taken in this country with respect to the control of transportation rates. I will show how this came about with respect to railway rates and hon. members will see whether or not there is any parallel between what- is now proposed and what was already done in that regard. As hon. gentlemen know, the Board of Railway Commissioners was established in 1903. Before 1903 there was no body controlling railway rates; the rates were left to the control of private companies as well as to such control as parliament exercised. We have heard a good deal lately in this House and in the country of an agreement passed in 1897, known as the Crowsnest pass agreement, which contained a (provision that if that subsidy was to be paid to the railway company the company, in return, was not to charge above certain rates with respect to certain commodities in western Canada. And we have seen hon. gentlemen of the Progres-
sive party upholding that agreement in the strangest possible terms. Now wherein is the difference between that principle and the present step which this government proposes in regard to the Petersen agreement? What *was done at that time was to give a subsidy to a railway, with a condition attached fixing the rates that should be charged on certain commodities over a certain territory. That was before there was any body established by parliament to control rates; and that was the step taken in 1897 some seven years before the railway commission itself came into being. It was a step, let me say, which served effectively in helping to bring about rate control; and this government at the present time in this proposal to parliament is simply following Liberal precedents. It was a Liberal government that established the Crowsnest pass agreement limited rate control and it was a Liberal government as well that established the railway commission to control rates. The present administration is following today precisely similar steps in regard to ocean rates, which to-day are under no control. We are taking as the first step the right to fix maximum rates on the ocean for certain commodities, giving a certain subsidy in return for that right. If the day comes, as my hon. friend in his amendment hopes, when there will be a commission controlling ocean rates, then it will be time to consider whether or not the step now taken has been adequate for the purpose it is intended to serve and has served its day and generation. But I submit to hon. gentlemen opposite that the course which the government is taking in this regard'is on all fours, with -respect to the controlling of ocean rates, with the step taken by the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier with a view to controlling certain railway -rates prior to the time the railway commission was created.
I would ask hon. gentlemen again to reflect that so far as this particular payment to be made to the Petersen company is concerned, it differs from the ordinary subsidy, so called, in being not merely a payment to a steamship line for certain services to be performed, but in being a payment for the right of the government to control the rates that shall apply to that service. At the present time we are paying a considerable subsidy to the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company, whose ships ply between Canada and the West Indies. That company receives annually the sum of $340,000, or $85,000 per ship; and that subsidy is paid simply for the service; it is not paid in return for the right of controlling rates, as is the case with the present contract.

Ocean Shipping Rates
Take the Union Steamship Company of New Zealand. That company now receives a subsidy of 1100,000 from this government, formerly it received $130,000. But in addition to that it receives a subsidy from New Zealand and one from Fiji, amounting to $219,000, or a subsidy per ship of $109,500, almost as great, when you reduce it to a rate per ship, as the subsidy we propose to pay the Petersen line, which is $130,000 per ship as figured out. And yet in the case of the Union company, plying between New Zealand and Canada, the subsidy is given simply for the running of the ships. In the present case the amount is paid only on condition that the ships shall carry the commodities at rates to be fixed under government control.

Yes. But I
would remind my hon. friend that he himself has not been far removed from suggesting precisely this method of dealing with transportation ratfes. He was complaining the other day that he had not an opportunity to bring before the House a resolution of his own which appears on the order paper. Let me read for him the last clause of that resolution :
That to enable [DOT] the products of the western and Maritime provinces to reach more readily the markets so developed the special transportation burdens borne by those provinces should be shared by the whole Dominion either by contribution to long haul freight costs or by assistance in some other form.
In other words, my right hon. friend suggests that this government should subsidize the railways for the long haul. What he has not brought out is the fact that while you may be helping the railways in that way, you are not necessarily helping the producing or consuming interests of this country. It has been pretty clearly demonstrated in this debate, that if every reduction of railway rates is to be offset by an increase in ocean rates, par-ticulary where the same company owns steamers as well as railways, the exporters of this country are not going to gain very much advantage. There is the crux of the whole situation. Reduce the rates on the ocean and you will find very soon that the export trade of this country will develop by leaps and bounds in a manner heretofore unknown. It is the high ocean rates which, to the disadvantage of exports, have been eating up
little by little all the advantages gained by control of railway rates.
I would ask hon. members to look at the terms of this contract. As drawn the country can lose nothing from any failure by the contractor. The worst that can happen is that we will be just where we are at present-still at the mercy of conditions as they are. On the other hand, if this contract is carried out from year to year, we will soon discover what is possible in the way of reduction of ocean rates. And once there begins to ply across the ocean a line of steamers on which the rates from Canada to the British Isles are at a particular figure, we will very soon see whether or not other shipping companies will not fall into line. I would add this further thought. There is no guarantee whatever, as matters stand, that further increases will not come rapidly upon the Atlantic. Here at least is one check in that regard. What does the contract state? First of all, that these ships shall ply between Canadian ports. That does not confine the service to Atlantic ports, it is equally applicable to Pacific ports.

I have spoken at very considerable length, and I think my hon. friend will forgive me if I do not go into that detail at the moment. Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw to a conclusion these lengthy remarks. They have been lengthy f"r the reason that I have been endeavouring to make it perfectly clear to the House and to the country that this matter which the government is undertaking is very much in the public interest and I am anxious that it should be adequately understood and appreciated in all its bearings.
I would like to point out that the government's policy with respect to the reduction of ocean rates is only part of the larger policy which the government has in view of building up the industries of this country along lines that indicate the greatest possibility of successful development. We are desirous of developing the production of our basic industries. We have sought to relieve the capital that is essential to the development of those industries from some of the taxation to which it has been subjected. We have been endeavouring to develop a vigorous immigration policy. But having regard to the figures I have quoted to-night with respect to immigrant rates, and to a comparison between what it costs to bring a family from the Old Country to settle in this country to-day and what it cost ten years ago, the difficulty with which the government has been confronted will be readily appreciated. The only way to overcome that difficulty is to grapple with the ocean rates on immigrants; if we are to be successful in getting immigrants into Canada we must take some step to control ocean rates. Then, we have affirmed the policy of endeavouring to develop Canadian trade through Canadian ports. We are spending large sums of money on the improvement and equipment of our ports. We are sincere in our desire to develop interimperial trade, to further the trade between Canada and the Mother Country, believing that to be in our mutual interests and believing it to be a link of empire which should be strengthened in every possible way. In addition to that we have sought to develop
our entire export trade in a manner that will help to build up our basic industries, our manufacturing industries, and the trade of the country generally.
The successful carrying out of all these policies, depends, I submit, upon such a reduction of ocean rates as will make the increase in the rates on the ocean during recent years, at least comparable to the increase that has taken place on the railways. So long as a conference framed among these shipping companies so regulates the rates that it pays shippers to ship via American ports; so fixes the rates as to make it impossible for many of our producers to ship via Canadian ports to the Old Country-so long as that condition prevails we may look in vain to all the other remedies that may be suggested for an improvement of our industrial condition.
We have to-day an opening in the British market for our cattle such as we have not had for twenty or thirty years, but we are prevented from getting the full advantage of that market simply because of the high ocean rates that are being charged; and what in that regard is true of cattle is true also of other commodities. Owing to the tariff wall which exists between the United States and this country we are prevented from selling cattle profitably across the line. There is a duty of as much as a cent to a cent and a half a pound, I understand, on lean cattle going into the American market. It does not pay to ship these cattle across the Atlantic at the rates fixed, although they are the class of cattle which are largely demanded by the British importers and would have a large market in Great Britain. We are restricted to the St. Lawrence route, to our Atlantic ports and our Pacific ports for the development of the trade of the country, but those ports will never be developed as they should, those industries will never prosper, unless by means of an adjustment of rates prevailing on the Atlantic we have an opportunity to compete successfully with other countries. Did time permit I could point out the effect of the present condition upon the chilled meat industry, which was lost to this country through American competition at one stage and which is lost to us to-day through competition from the Argentine and Uruguay, whence frozen meats can be shipped to Britain at the lower rates prevailing from those countries-rates fixed by this north Atlantic combine. If we are in earnest in the desire to build up Canadian industry, in seeking to develop our agriculture, lumber, mining, fishing resources, as well as our manufacturing industries, which are dependent

upon the development of the basic industries but equally dependent upon the markets they have abroad, I submit that we must take such steps as are possible at this time to reduce ocean rates.
Hon. gentlemen opposite say this is a small step; that it is inadequate; that it is not large enough to be effective. I would remind hon. members of the biblical narrative of David and Goliath. It was not the size of David or the size of the pebble that brought about the result that was effected at that time. It was the accuracy of the throw. It so happened that the aim that was taken was the right one; the giant was hit in a vital spot. If I am not mistaken, the pebble that has been thrown into the Atlantic by this much abused report of Mr. Preston and by the discussion which we are having in this parliament at the present time; the pebble that has been thrown into the Atlantic by the step which this government has taken, has stirred the waters of all the seas to the shores of every country to which the operations of this combine extend. How are the correspondents
paid? Are they paid according to the copy they send in, or what is the basis of their remuneration?
They are paid an annual salary, somewhat proportionate to the importance of the place where the correspondent is located. I might give my hon. friend an indication of how the salary varies.
Give us the extremes.

I might mention Thet-ford Mines $150. The sum of $125 is the very minimum. We find $125 paid at Sherbrooke. Then at a place like Timmins, up in the mining region, the amount is $200, and at Halifax, N.S., $225. The salary paid at Trail, B.C. is $300, the understanding being that at Trail there is a pretty wide range of territory to cover, and there are a number of different little centres where it is necessary for the correspondent to get reasonably accurate information and send it in. That is the basis upon which the salary is determined.
That is through the monthly report?
The monthly report.
Is the report sent in for a particular month or is that left to the correspondent?

No the department expects the correspondent to send in a report each month.

Will the minister tell us what saving has been effected by having this publication printed at the bureau instead of parties outside?

Well there was a difference between the printing of the Labour Gazette in the Printing Bureau in 1924 and the outside printing in 1923. In saying that I am taking into consideration the smaller type now used, because we changed the type used in printing the Labour Gazette from 10 point to 9 point type when we started to print it in the bureau. Then we condensed the report, there were a smaller number of pages than in 1923, so that there was a saving for the year of S13,704.31.
It was really a saving in the paper used, not in the composition?
Yes there is less paper. In the annual bound report I think there are about 346 pages less. Smaller type is used and there are fewer pages. There is not as much matter in the Labour Gazette now.
Has there been a saving in the cost of printing? I can understand there would be a saving in the matter of paper, but I cannot understand how there would be any saving in composition?
There would not be a saving in composition for a page merely, but there would be a considerable saving in paper.
I think the minister pointed out that there was a decrease of $11,000, so practically that would be accounted for by the very item we are now discussing?
Yes.

It seems to me, if my memory serves me correctly, that in 1922, it may have been 1923, there were some questions asked the minister regarding a contract he then made with, I think, a new corporation. If I remember rightly I think he gave a very good reason for the change; I think he was very frank and said it was on account of some very good Liberals. I am not finding any fault with that statement now, but what I should like to know is if it is a fact that this saving of $11,000 is the difference between the present cost of printing the Labour Gazette at the Printing Bureau and the amount he was paying the firm with whom he made that contract in 1922 or 1923-I forget the exact year?

No, I think my hon. friend is just a little off as to the facts. A 81i
contract was given to an outside firm to print the Labour Gazette in 1922 on the same basis on which it had been printed for many years, all during the term of the government my hon. friend supported, only in a different form-the basis of payment was identically the same but the bureau rates, I think, were 10 per cent less.

The minister misunderstood me. I did not charge him with paying any more to this company he dealt with in 1922 than had been paid previously; what I was trying to find out was whether the saving of $11,000 is due to the fact that the Gazette is printed at the Printing Bureau. Taking into consideration the smaller type that we have, now does that account for it?	,

My hon. friend possibly did not hear me when I read this before. I will read it again. The amount requested, $35,000, is $11,000 less than the amount voted for the fiscal year 1924-25. The appropriation is intended mainly to meet the cost of the printing, binding and distribution of the Labour Gazette. From this appropriation are paid the salaries of some sixty to seventy persons employed as correspondents, with salaries ranging from $125 to $300 per annum. I agree with the hon.

Conciliation and Labour Act, including publishing, printing, binding and distribution of the Labour Gazette and allowance to correspondents, and to provide for the payment of the salary of the private secretary of the minister.

I think the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) asked what was paid to the representative at Sydney and I do not think that was answered. It would strike me that he would be a very busy agent and it would be interesting if we had his correspondence. Is he still working on it now?
We have no representative at Sydney.
Would that not be a most important place to have one?

If the idea is to help in labour matters would it not be a good thing to have the work done where there is real necessity for it? If there is one place where such work is needed it is at Glace Bay.

I agree that there is no place in Canada where there is greater necessity for work to be done tihan in the vicinity of Glace Bay, and that has been the condition for several years. But no one knows better than my hon. friend what the extent of authority of the Labour department' is in a matter of this kind. I can assure him, however, that we took every possible step that could have been taken. My hon. friend will agree with that, I think. And even when the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act was declared ultra vires we endeavoured to form a board which we hoped would be able to assist in bringing about harmony and cooperation and if possible a settlement.
You have as much authority there as anywhere else in Canada.
Under certain conditions possibly, yes; under other conditions, as my hon. friend knows, we have not.
I know that, and I should like to have an explanation.

In the steel plant at
Sydney or at New Glasgow or at the Sault, if a dispute occurred years ago before the act was placed in its present position we should never have claimed any authority to deal with the trouble. If by offering our friendly offices we could do anything to promote harmony we would do it. But as to authority, we had none and never claimed to have it. As to the dispute in the coal mines, it was held to come under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act; but as my hon. friend knows, that is altogether a matter of uncertainty. It has been merely a question of trying to do whatever appeared possible to bring about a settlement.

I have been considering the Labour Gazette from the standpoint of education. I do not know whether this is any part of its function, but if it is not I cannot see that the Gazette has any function. I should think that its chief function would be to gather information of a sociological character.
Sociological?

An hon. gentleman opposite evidently has not heard that word; it is really one of the most important words to-day, for sociology is a coming science. I should -like to think that the Labour Gazette was trying
to perform a service along that line, and I do not think that there is any place in Canada where the labour problem is more acute than it is in that part of the Maritime provinces. Certainly the labour problem has not been more acute in the past few years anywhere than in the point which has been mentioned, and I should think that it would be eminently advisable to have a representative of the Labour Gazette there, who, even though he might not be permanent, could obtain all the data and information bearing upon the particular social phenomenon that we see there now. That information would be indispensable to the Labour department. I hope the minister will consider putting one of his officers there to collect such facts as are relevant to the whole matter, if that is part of the function of the publication.

The hon. gentleman
may be under a misapprehension. There is a Labour Gazette correspondent at Sydney but his duty is not to write on sociological questions; it is confined to the securing of prices and to the giving of advice from time to time as to labour unrest or labour conditions generally. He deals only with such facts as are apparent and in evidence. There has been a Labour Gazette correspondent although he is not regarded as an employee of the department. He might be called a part time employee from the fact that every month he sends in a report to the department. Presumably he is collecting or verifying material for the report during the rest of the month.

What is his qualification?
Is he appointed from the standpoint of a journalist?

In a number of cases. I think I am safe in saying, our best correspondents have been or are journalists; in other cases they have been representatives of labour for a number of years in some local capacity, having shown a sympathetic ability to grasp the questions with which they have to deal. I am not sure how many, but possibly there are six or eight or more newspaper men.

Is there any connection
between the Department of Labour and the Bureau of Statistics? Is there any duplication of work?

In some respects there is a degree of co-operation between the two departments. The Conciliation and Labour Act, as my hon. friend knows, defines the duties of the Labour department in- regard to certain statistics on labour matters. These figures and facts have always been collected

by the Department of Labour. There is an able staff in the department who can more sympathetically and with greater accuracy compile them. The figures in regard to prices are brought into the Labour department and then they are passed over to the Bureau of Statistics where they are analyzed and compiled and issued each month. They are later copied into the Labour Gazette and become part of the official record. There is co-operation in that way.
